chapters.n: Second Nephi opens with Lehi’s final counsel to his family. Nephi introduces it: after Nephi taught his brothers, the aging Lehi recounted the great things God had done in bringing them out of Jerusalem.

f.g: Recounted, went over again.

chapters.n: Lehi reminds them of their rebellion on the ship and God’s mercy in sparing their lives during the storm.
He speaks of the promised land and of the Lord’s mercy in warning them to flee Jerusalem.

f.w: warning us that we should flee

chapters.n: Lehi has seen in vision that Jerusalem has been destroyed. Had they stayed, they would have died. Babylon destroyed the city in 587/586 BC.
Despite their trials, they have received a land “choice above all other lands,” covenanted to Lehi’s descendants forever and to all whom the Lord leads there from other countries.
Lehi prophesies that no one will come to this land unless the Lord brings them. Its settlement is under God’s hand.

f.w: brought by the hand of the Lord

chapters.n: The land is dedicated to those God brings. If they keep His commandments it will be a land of liberty and they will never be enslaved; but if wickedness spreads, the land will be cursed for them. Freedom is tied to righteousness.

f.g: Set apart, dedicated for a holy purpose.

chapters.n: For now it is wise to keep the land hidden from other nations, or they would overrun it and leave no room for Lehi’s descendants.

f.w: kept as yet from the knowledge of other nations

chapters.n: Lehi’s covenant promise: if those God brings from Jerusalem keep His commandments, they will prosper, be protected from other nations, and live safely forever.

f.g: Trouble, harass, attack.

chapters.n: But if they reject Christ after receiving so much — knowledge of creation, God’s works, power through faith, all the commandments, a choice land — then justice will fall on them. Greater light brings greater accountability.

f.w: the true Messiah, their Redeemer and their God

chapters.n: God will bring other nations against them, take away their lands, and scatter them — prophecies fulfilled when the Nephites fell and Lehi’s remaining descendants suffered at the hands of later nations.

f.w: he will bring other nations unto them

chapters.n: Generations will see bloodshed and divine judgments. Lehi pleads with his sons to remember and listen.

f.g: Divine judgments or punishments.

chapters.n: Lehi’s emotional plea: wake up from the deep sleep of hell and shake off the awful chains of sin that drag people down to misery. Sin is pictured as both sleep and slavery.

Lehi calls himself a “trembling parent” who will soon be buried in the grave, “from whence no traveler can return” — wording similar to a line in Shakespeare’s Hamlet. He is about to go “the way of all the earth,” meaning death.

f.w: the way of all the earth

chapters.n: Even facing death, Lehi testifies with joy: the Lord has redeemed his soul, he has seen His glory, and he is eternally encircled in the arms of His love.

f.w: encircled about eternally in the arms of his love

chapters.n: His lifelong concern has been that his children keep the Lord’s statutes and judgments.
Lehi has often been heavy with sorrow, afraid that his sons’ hard hearts will bring God’s full wrath and destruction on them.
He also fears a curse lasting many generations — war, famine, hatred, and captivity to the devil.
Lehi wishes they could be a choice and favored people. Yet he submits: God’s will be done, for His ways are always right.
Lehi repeats the core promise of the Book of Mormon: keep the commandments and prosper; disobey and be cut off from God’s presence.

f.w: Inasmuch as ye shall keep my commandments ye shall prosper in the land

chapters.n: So that he can die with joy rather than grief, Lehi urges his sons to rise up, be men, and be united in one mind and heart.

f.w: one mind and in one heart

chapters.n: Unity and obedience would protect them from a severe curse and from God’s just displeasure that could destroy both body and soul.

f.g: Severe curse.

chapters.n: Lehi gives a series of commands: wake up, put on the armor of righteousness, shake off chains, come out of obscurity, and rise from the dust. Isaiah used similar words calling Zion to awake.
Lehi defends Nephi: he has kept the commandments, been God’s instrument in bringing them to the promised land, and saved them from starving — yet they tried to kill him.

f.w: instrument in the hands of God

chapters.n: Lehi fears Nephi will suffer again at their hands. They have accused Nephi of wanting power, but Lehi testifies Nephi sought only God’s glory and their eternal welfare.

f.w: sought power and authority over you

chapters.n: They complained that Nephi was blunt and angry. Lehi explains it was the power of God’s word in him — truth that could not be held back as he boldly named their sins.
God’s power had to be with Nephi; it was the Spirit within him, not Nephi himself, that opened his mouth so he could not stay silent.
If Laman, Lemuel, Sam, and Ishmael’s sons will listen to Nephi, they will not perish, and Lehi will give them his “first blessing” — the birthright blessing normally due the eldest son.

f.g: The birthright blessing, traditionally given to the firstborn son.

chapters.n: But if they refuse, Lehi will take the first blessing away and give it to Nephi — echoing how leadership passed from Reuben to Joseph in Israel’s history.
Lehi now addresses Zoram, once Laban’s servant, who joined the family on the way out of Jerusalem. Lehi calls him Nephi’s true friend forever.
Because Zoram has been faithful, his descendants will prosper alongside Nephi’s in the land, and only their own wickedness can disturb that. The Zoramites appear later in Nephite history.

f.w: thy seed shall be blessed with his seed

chapters.n: If Zoram’s descendants keep the commandments, the Lord has consecrated the land for their security together with Nephi’s descendants.
Lehi now blesses Jacob, his first son born in the wilderness. As a child Jacob suffered because of his older brothers’ harshness.

f.w: my firstborn in the days of my tribulation

f.g: Harshness, cruelty.

chapters.n: Jacob knows God’s greatness, and Lehi promises that God will “consecrate” his afflictions — turn his suffering into something sacred and beneficial.

f.w: he shall consecrate thine afflictions for thy gain

chapters.n: Jacob will be blessed, live safely with Nephi, and serve God all his days. Lehi knows Jacob is redeemed — not by Jacob’s own goodness, but by the righteousness of his Redeemer, whom Jacob has seen will come.

f.w: because of the righteousness of thy Redeemer

f.g: The appointed time in God’s plan.

chapters.n: Jacob saw Christ’s glory as a youth, so he is as blessed as those who will see Christ in mortality. The Spirit is unchanging. Since the Fall, the way back has been prepared, and salvation is “free” — offered as a gift to all.

f.w: thou hast beheld in thy youth his glory

chapters.n: People know good from evil, and God has given law. But no one is made right with God by the law alone, because everyone breaks it. Under both temporal and spiritual law, people are cut off and become miserable.

f.w: instructed sufficiently that they know good from evil
by the law no flesh is justified

chapters.n: So redemption comes only through the Holy Messiah, who is full of grace and truth.
Christ offered Himself as a sacrifice for sin to satisfy the demands of the law — for all who have a broken heart and a contrite spirit. Repentance opens the door to His Atonement.

f.w: answer the ends of the law
f.g: Satisfy the law’s requirements (justice).

f.w: a broken heart and a contrite spirit

chapters.n: How important it is to teach everyone that no one can live with God except through Christ’s merits, mercy, and grace. He lays down His life and takes it up again, bringing about the resurrection as the first to rise.
Christ is the “firstfruits” — the first of the harvest of the resurrection. He intercedes, or pleads, for all people, and those who believe in Him will be saved.

f.g: The first part of a harvest, offered to God; here, the first to be resurrected.

chapters.n: Because of Christ’s intercession, all people return to God to be judged by Him. Punishment and happiness are both “affixed” — attached as consequences — to the law, and both serve the purposes of the Atonement. The sentence continues into the next verse.

f.g: Attached as the set consequence.

chapters.n: A foundational idea: there must be opposition in all things. Without opposites, there could be no righteousness or wickedness, joy or misery. Everything would be one undivided “compound,” lifeless and meaningless.

f.g: A single undifferentiated mass, with no contrasts.

chapters.n: Such a world would have been created for nothing, with no purpose — which would undermine God’s wisdom, purposes, power, mercy, and justice.

f.g: Something worthless or pointless.

chapters.n: A chain of logic: no law means no sin; no sin, no righteousness; no righteousness, no happiness; and without these there is no God — and nothing would exist at all. Moral law and existence itself are tied together.

f.w: to act nor to be acted upon

chapters.n: But there is a God. He created the heavens and the earth and everything in them — both things that act (agents) and things that are acted upon.
To accomplish His purposes for humanity, God placed opposition in Eden: the forbidden fruit opposite the tree of life, one sweet and one bitter.

f.w: the forbidden fruit in opposition to the tree of life

chapters.n: God gave humanity agency — the power to act for themselves. But real choice requires being “enticed” by both good and evil.

f.g: Attracted, drawn toward.

chapters.n: From scripture, Lehi concludes that an angel of God fell from heaven and became the devil by seeking evil.

Having become miserable, the devil wants everyone to be miserable. As the serpent and “father of all lies,” he told Eve she would not die but would become like God, knowing good and evil — a half-truth wrapped around a lie.
After eating the forbidden fruit, Adam and Eve were sent out of Eden to work the ground.

f.w: driven out of the garden of Eden

chapters.n: They had children — the whole human family.

f.w: the family of all the earth

chapters.n: God lengthened human life so people could repent while in mortality. Life became a “state of probation” — a test. All must repent, because the Fall left everyone lost.
Had Adam not transgressed, he and Eve would have stayed in Eden, and everything would have remained unchanged forever. Latter-day Saints often distinguish this “transgression” from sin.
They would have had no children and stayed innocent — with no joy because they knew no misery, and doing no good because they knew no sin.

f.w: they would have had no children

chapters.n: All this happened according to the wisdom of God, who knows all things. The Fall was part of His plan, not a failure of it.

f.w: the wisdom of him who knoweth all things

chapters.n: One of the best-known verses in the Book of Mormon: Adam fell so that humanity could exist, and people exist so that they can have joy. Joy is the purpose of our existence.

f.w: Adam fell that men might be

chapters.n: The Messiah will come to redeem humanity from the Fall. Redeemed, people are forever free to act for themselves rather than being acted upon — accountable only to God’s law at the last day.

f.w: to act for themselves and not to be acted upon

chapters.n: Because of Christ, people are free to choose liberty and eternal life through Him, the great Mediator, or captivity and death through the devil, who wants everyone to be as miserable as he is.

f.w: free to choose liberty and eternal life

f.g: One who stands between two parties to reconcile them.

chapters.n: Lehi pleads with his sons to look to the Mediator, obey His commandments, and choose eternal life by following the Holy Spirit.
Don’t choose eternal death by following the flesh and its evil, which gives the devil power to drag you down and rule over you.

f.g: Take captive.

chapters.n: Near the end of his life, Lehi says he has “chosen the good part” — echoing scripture — and his only aim is his sons’ eternal welfare.
Lehi turns to his youngest son, Joseph, born in the wilderness during Lehi’s hardest years.
Lehi prays that the Lord will dedicate this precious land as an inheritance for Joseph and his descendants alongside his brothers — if they keep the commandments.

f.g: Dedicate, set apart as sacred.

chapters.n: Lehi blesses Joseph forever and promises that his descendants will never be completely destroyed.

f.w: thy seed shall not utterly be destroyed

chapters.n: Lehi reveals that he descends from Joseph who was sold into Egypt — through Manasseh — and that the Lord made great covenants with that ancient Joseph.

Joseph of Egypt saw the latter days and was promised that God would raise a righteous branch from his descendants — not the Messiah, but a branch broken off (Lehi’s family). Christ would reveal Himself to them in the last days, bringing them from darkness to light.

f.w: a branch which was to be broken off

chapters.n: Joseph prophesied of a “choice seer” whom the Lord would raise up from his descendants. Latter-day Saints understand this seer to be Joseph Smith.

f.g: One who sees by divine power — a prophet who can reveal past and future.

chapters.n: The Lord told Joseph that this seer would be highly esteemed among Joseph’s descendants and would do a great work for them, teaching them God’s covenants with their fathers.

f.g: Joseph Smith’s inspired revision of the Bible (JST Genesis 50) restores a parallel version of this prophecy.

chapters.n: The seer will do only the work God commands, and God will make him great because he does God’s work.
He will be great like Moses, the deliverer of Israel.
Joseph of Egypt foresaw Moses, who would lead Israel out of Egypt.

f.w: deliver thy people out of the land of Egypt

chapters.n: The latter-day seer will bring forth God’s word to Joseph’s descendants — and also help convince them of the word they already have, the Bible.

Joseph’s descendants will write (the Book of Mormon), and Judah’s descendants will write (the Bible). These records will “grow together” to refute false doctrines, end contention, and bring peace and knowledge of God’s covenants.
The seer will be made strong out of weakness when God’s work of restoring Israel begins. Joseph Smith was an uneducated farm boy when called.

f.w: out of weakness he shall be made strong

chapters.n: Joseph prophesied that the Lord would bless the seer and confound those who tried to destroy him. Joseph of Egypt was certain this promise would be fulfilled.

f.w: they that seek to destroy him shall be confounded

chapters.n: The seer’s name would be Joseph, like his father’s — Joseph Smith Jr. was named after his father, Joseph Smith Sr. What he brings forth by God’s power will bring Joseph’s people to salvation.

f.w: his name shall be called after me

chapters.n: Joseph is as sure of this as of the promise about Moses. God promised to preserve his descendants forever.

f.w: I will preserve thy seed forever

chapters.n: God promised to raise a Moses with power in his rod and judgment in writing. Moses would not be eloquent, so God would write His law with His own finger and give Moses a spokesman — Aaron.

f.w: I will not make him mighty in speaking
by the finger of mine own hand

chapters.n: Likewise God would raise up the latter-day seer with a spokesman. The seer would write (translate) the record of Joseph’s descendants, and a spokesman would declare it. Latter-day revelation names Sidney Rigdon as a spokesman to Joseph Smith.

f.w: I will make for him a spokesman

chapters.n: The seer will write what God in His wisdom wants Joseph’s descendants to have. It will be as if their ancestors cried to them “from the dust” — an image of a voice from buried records.

f.w: cried unto them from the dust

chapters.n: These ancient voices will cry repentance to their descendants many generations later, and their message will go forth because of its simplicity.
Because of the ancient writers’ faith, God will make their weak words strong, to help their descendants remember His covenants.

f.w: the weakness of their words will I make strong

chapters.n: Lehi tells his son Joseph that this is how their ancestor prophesied.

f.g: Joseph of Egypt, Lehi’s ancestor.

chapters.n: Because of this covenant, young Joseph is blessed: his descendants will not be destroyed, because they will listen to the words of the book.
One mighty in word and deed will rise among them, an instrument in God’s hands with great faith, bringing much restoration to Israel. Many Latter-day Saints apply this, too, to Joseph Smith.

f.w: an instrument in the hands of God

chapters.n: Lehi tells young Joseph, still a child, to listen to his brother Nephi, and these blessings will be fulfilled. He asks Joseph to remember his dying father’s words.

f.g: You are young.

f.w: hearken unto the words of thy brother, Nephi

chapters.n: Nephi comments on the prophecies of Joseph of Egypt that Lehi had just recited.

f.w: Joseph, who was carried into Egypt

chapters.n: Joseph prophesied about all his descendants, and few prophecies are greater. His writings, which included prophecies about Lehi’s people, were on the brass plates but are not in our Bible.

f.w: they are written upon the plates of brass

chapters.n: Lehi gathers Laman’s children to bless them, calling them the children of his firstborn.
Lehi repeats the Lord’s core promise: keep the commandments and prosper; disobey and be cut off from His presence.

f.w: ye shall prosper in the land

chapters.n: Lehi cannot die without blessing these grandchildren. He knows that children raised in the right way will not leave it.

f.w: brought up in the way ye should go

chapters.n: If these children are cursed because of their parents’ choices, Lehi blesses them so the curse may rest on the parents instead. Children are not held responsible for their parents’ sins.

f.w: be answered upon the heads of your parents

chapters.n: Because of this blessing, God will not allow them to perish and will be merciful to their descendants forever.

f.w: he will be merciful unto you and unto your seed forever

chapters.n: Next, Lehi calls Lemuel’s children before him.
He gives them the same blessing: they will not be entirely destroyed, and in the end their descendants will be blessed.

f.w: in the end thy seed shall be blessed

chapters.n: Lehi then speaks to Ishmael’s sons and their entire household. Their words are not recorded.
Lehi blesses Sam: he will inherit the land like Nephi, and his descendants will be counted with Nephi’s. Sam, the quiet faithful brother, shares Nephi’s blessings.
After blessing his whole household according to his heart and the Spirit, Lehi grows old, dies, and is buried. A great patriarch’s life ends.

f.g: Grew old.

chapters.n: Soon after Lehi’s death, Laman, Lemuel, and Ishmael’s sons grow angry with Nephi because of the Lord’s warnings he delivered.

f.g: Warnings, reproofs.

chapters.n: Nephi felt compelled to speak to them by the Lord’s word. Much of what was said is recorded on his other (large) plates, which contain more history.

f.g: Compelled, urged.

chapters.n: On these small plates Nephi writes the “things of my soul” and scriptures from the brass plates. He loves the scriptures, ponders them, and writes them for his children. This introduces what is often called the “Psalm of Nephi.”

f.w: my soul delighteth in the scriptures

chapters.n: Nephi delights in the things of the Lord and constantly ponders what he has seen and heard.
Despite God’s goodness, Nephi cries out, “O wretched man that I am!” He grieves over his weaknesses and sins. Even great prophets feel their imperfections deeply — Paul uses the same words.

f.w: O wretched man that I am

chapters.n: Nephi feels surrounded by temptations and sins that “easily beset” him — that cling and trip him up.

f.g: Surrounded on all sides.

chapters.n: When he wants to rejoice, his heart groans over his sins — yet he knows whom he has trusted. That turning point changes everything.

f.w: I know in whom I have trusted

chapters.n: Nephi remembers God’s past help: support in trials, guidance through the wilderness, and protection on the ocean. Remembering builds hope.

f.w: the waters of the great deep

chapters.n: God has filled him with love so intensely that his body could barely bear it.
God confounded his enemies until they trembled before him.
God heard his cries by day and gave him visions by night.
In bold, mighty prayer Nephi has called on God, and angels have come down to minister to him.
Carried by the Spirit to high mountains, Nephi saw things too great for man to write.
Then why, having seen so much of God’s mercy, should he linger in sorrow and lose strength because of trials? Nephi questions his own discouragement.
Why give in to sin and temptation and let the evil one destroy his peace? Why be angry with his enemy? Nephi identifies anger as part of his struggle.

f.w: Why am I angry because of mine enemy?

chapters.n: Nephi rallies himself: “Awake, my soul!” He commands his heart to rejoice and give no place to the enemy.

f.w: give place no more for the enemy

chapters.n: He resolves not to be angry with enemies or lose strength because of afflictions.
He calls his heart to rejoice and praise the Lord forever, “the rock of my salvation.”
Nephi prays: redeem my soul, deliver me from my enemies, and make me “shake at the appearance of sin” — so sensitive that even the hint of sin makes him recoil.

f.w: shake at the appearance of sin

chapters.n: Nephi asks that hell’s gates stay shut to him because his heart is broken and his spirit contrite. He also asks God to keep him enclosed within “the gates of thy righteousness,” so he can walk the humble low road and stay strictly on the plain path.

f.w: my heart is broken and my spirit is contrite

f.g: A humble path, in contrast to proud heights.

chapters.n: Nephi asks to be wrapped in the “robe of righteousness,” to have an escape from enemies, a straight path, and no stumbling blocks — and for God to block his enemy’s way instead of his.

f.g: Don’t block my path with obstacles.

chapters.n: Nephi will trust God forever and never put his trust in the “arm of flesh” — human strength — for those who do are cursed.
God gives generously to those who ask, as long as they don’t ask for the wrong things. So Nephi will keep crying to God, his rock, forever.

f.w: God will give liberally to him that asketh

chapters.n: Nephi prays often and earnestly because of his brothers’ anger after Lehi’s death.
Their anger grows until they plan to kill him.

f.w: seek to take away my life

chapters.n: They resent their younger brother leading them and claim the right to rule belongs to the older brothers. This grievance over birthright will fuel Lamanite hostility for centuries.

f.w: it belongs unto us, who are the elder brethren

chapters.n: Nephi doesn’t record all their complaints; it is enough to say they sought his life.
The Lord warns Nephi to flee into the wilderness with everyone willing to follow him.
Nephi leaves with his family, Zoram, Sam, Jacob, Joseph, his sisters, and all who believed God’s revelations. This verse is the only mention of Nephi’s sisters.

f.g: Nephi’s sisters are mentioned only here.

chapters.n: They take their tents and belongings and travel many days before settling.
The people choose to name the new place Nephi, after their leader. The land and city of Nephi become important in later history.
Those with Nephi call themselves the “people of Nephi” — the Nephites.
They carefully keep the law of Moses in all things. As Nephi later explains, they kept it while looking forward to Christ.

f.w: according to the law of Moses

chapters.n: The Lord blesses them: their crops yield abundantly and they raise flocks and herds.
Nephi brought the brass plates and the Liahona — the sacred records and the guide God gave Lehi.
The people prosper and grow in number.
Knowing his brothers’ hatred, Nephi makes swords patterned after Laban’s sword to defend his people. Laban’s sword became a sacred heirloom.

f.g: The followers of Laman — first named as a people here.

chapters.n: Nephi teaches his people construction and metalwork in wood, iron, copper, brass, steel, gold, silver, and other ores.
Nephi builds a temple modeled on Solomon’s temple, though with fewer precious materials. Even in a new land, the temple stands at the center of their worship.

f.w: I, Nephi, did build a temple

chapters.n: Nephi teaches his people to be industrious and to work with their hands.

f.g: Hardworking, diligent.

chapters.n: The people want Nephi to be their king. He prefers they have no king, but he serves them as best he can. Later Nephite kings take the title “second Nephi,” “third Nephi,” and so on.

f.w: they would that I should be their king

chapters.n: The Lord’s promise that Nephi would rule and teach his brothers was fulfilled — until they tried to kill him.
Another promise was fulfilled: because the brothers would not listen, they were cut off from the Lord’s presence.

f.w: cut off from the presence of the Lord

chapters.n: The central point is that the Lamanites were cut off because they hardened their hearts “like unto a flint.” The verse also mentions a skin of blackness set as a mark of separation. The Church today teaches that dark skin is not a sign of divine disfavor or a curse, and it disavows past theories that taught otherwise.

f.g: Flint is a very hard stone — an image of a heart that will not soften.

chapters.n: God says the Lamanites will be repellent to the Nephites unless they repent — a social and spiritual barrier meant to keep the two peoples separate while the Lamanites rejected God.
Anyone who joins with the Lamanites would share their condition. The concern is religious: joining those who rejected God meant rejecting Him too.
Separated from God, the Lamanites became idle and full of mischief and cunning, hunting wild animals in the wilderness instead of farming.

f.g: Craftiness, cunning.

chapters.n: The Lord tells Nephi the Lamanites will be a “scourge” to the Nephites — a whip to stir them to remember God. If the Nephites forget Him, the Lamanites will destroy them, as eventually happened.

f.w: They shall be a scourge unto thy seed

chapters.n: Nephi consecrates his younger brothers Jacob and Joseph as priests and teachers over the people.
A simple, beautiful summary: “we lived after the manner of happiness.” Righteous living, honest work, temple worship, and unity bring happiness.
Thirty years have passed since leaving Jerusalem — roughly 570 BC.

f.g: About 570 BC by the Book of Mormon’s reckoning.

chapters.n: Nephi had kept the history of his people on the plates he made earlier (the large plates).
The Lord commands Nephi to make other plates for things good in His sight, for his people’s benefit — the small plates.
Nephi obeys and makes the plates on which he writes this record.
He engraves what is pleasing to God. Those who love the things of God will love these writings.
For detailed history, readers should look to the other plates.
Forty years have passed, and wars with the Lamanites have already begun — a sad note after the “manner of happiness.”

f.w: wars and contentions with our brethren

chapters.n: A new section begins: a sermon by Jacob, Nephi’s younger brother, to the Nephites. It runs through chapter 10.
Jacob establishes his authority: called by God, ordained in His holy order, and consecrated by Nephi, whom the people regard as a king and protector.

f.g: The holy priesthood after the order of the Son of God.

chapters.n: Jacob is deeply concerned for his people’s souls. He has taught them Lehi’s words and all the scriptures from the Creation onward.

f.w: mine anxiety is great for you

chapters.n: Now he will speak of present and future events by reading Isaiah, as Nephi asked, so they may learn and glorify God.
Isaiah spoke to all Israel, so his words can be applied to the Nephites, who are part of Israel.
Jacob quotes Isaiah 49:22: God will raise a banner to the Gentiles, who will carry Israel’s children home. Nephi quoted the same passage earlier.
Isaiah 49:23: kings and queens will nurture Israel, and those who wait on the Lord will not be ashamed.
Jacob now explains: the Lord has shown him that the people of Jerusalem have been killed and taken captive to Babylon.
They will return. Then the Holy One of Israel will come to them in the flesh, and they will scourge and crucify Him. Jacob learned this from an angel.
After they harden their hearts against Him, judgments will come upon them.

f.g: Became stubborn, refusing to bow.

chapters.n: They will be driven about and afflicted, yet not allowed to perish completely because of the prayers of the faithful. When they come to know their Redeemer, they will be gathered to their promised lands.

f.w: because of the prayers of the faithful

chapters.n: Gentiles who repent, don’t fight Zion, and don’t join the great and abominable church will be saved. God will keep His covenants.
Those who fight Zion will be humbled, but the Lord’s people will not be ashamed. They are those who “wait for him” — still awaiting the Messiah.

Quoting Isaiah 11:11, Jacob says the Messiah will “set himself again the second time” to recover Israel — the latter-day gathering. He will come in power and glory and destroy none who believe in Him.
Those who do not believe will be destroyed by fire, storms, earthquakes, bloodshed, plague, and famine — and all will know the Lord is God.

f.w: by fire, and by tempest, and by earthquakes

chapters.n: Jacob quotes Isaiah 49:24: can captives be taken from a mighty warrior?
Yes — the Mighty God will free His covenant people. Jacob’s version reads “the Mighty God shall deliver his covenant people,” a phrase not in the KJV of Isaiah 49:25.

f.w: the Mighty God shall deliver his covenant people
f.g: Wording unique to the Book of Mormon, not in KJV Isaiah 49:25.

chapters.n: Israel’s oppressors will turn on themselves, and all will know the Lord is Israel’s Savior, Redeemer, and the Mighty One of Jacob. Jacob continues Isaiah in the next chapters.

Jacob continues with Isaiah 50. The Lord asks Israel: did I divorce you or sell you to pay a debt? No — Israel’s own sins caused the separation. The Book of Mormon adds an opening question, “have I cast thee off forever?”, sharpening the point that God has not abandoned them.

f.g: A legal divorce certificate under the law of Moses.

f.w: for your iniquities have ye sold yourselves

chapters.n: When the Lord came, no one answered. Yet His arm is not too short to save. He who can dry up the sea and rivers by His command can certainly redeem Israel. The Book of Mormon makes the first lines statements rather than questions and adds “O house of Israel.”
God can darken the heavens as if dressed in sackcloth, the rough cloth worn in mourning. Some see a foreshadowing of the darkness at Christ’s death.

f.g: Coarse, dark goat-hair cloth worn in grief or repentance.

f.w: I clothe the heavens with blackness

chapters.n: Now the Servant speaks. God gave Him a trained tongue to speak the right word to the weary, and wakes Him each morning to listen like a disciple. Christians see Jesus here, whose words strengthened the weary.

f.g: The tongue of one who has been taught — a disciple’s tongue.

chapters.n: The Servant listened and did not rebel or turn back — perfect obedience.
The Servant willingly endured beating, having His beard torn, shame, and spitting. This matches Jesus’ sufferings before His crucifixion in striking detail.

f.w: I gave my back to the smiter

f.g: Tore out the beard — a deep insult.

chapters.n: Because God helps Him, the Servant will not be put to shame. He sets His face “like a flint” — unshakably determined.

f.w: set my face like a flint

chapters.n: The Lord is near and will vindicate Him. Who dares accuse Him? The Book of Mormon adds that He will strike His adversary with the strength of His mouth — His word.
All who condemn the Servant will wear out like an old moth-eaten garment.
Who among you fears the Lord, obeys His servant, yet walks in darkness without light? The Book of Mormon ends the verse here, without the KJV’s added counsel to “trust in the name of the Lord.”
Those who try to light their own way — relying on their own “sparks” rather than God’s light — will lie down in sorrow.

f.w: walk in the light of your fire

chapters.n: Jacob continues with Isaiah 51. To those who seek righteousness, the Lord says: remember where you came from — the “rock” and “quarry” you were cut from.

f.w: the rock from whence ye are hewn
f.g: Your origin — explained in the next verse as Abraham and Sarah.

chapters.n: Abraham and Sarah are Israel’s ancestors. God called Abraham alone and blessed him with countless descendants, so He can surely restore Israel now.
The Lord will comfort Zion and turn her ruins into a garden like Eden, full of joy, thanks, and music.
God calls His people to listen: His law and justice will go out as a light to all people.
His righteousness and salvation are near. His “arm” — His power — will judge, and distant lands will trust in it.

f.g: God’s power to act and save.
Distant coastlands and peoples.

chapters.n: Heaven and earth will pass away like smoke and wear out like a garment, but God’s salvation lasts forever.

f.w: the heavens shall vanish away like smoke

chapters.n: To those with God’s law written on their hearts: don’t fear people’s scorn or insults.

f.w: in whose heart I have written my law

f.g: Abusive insults.

chapters.n: Scoffers will be eaten away like wool by moths, but God’s righteousness endures through all generations.

f.w: the moth shall eat them up

chapters.n: The people cry for God to awake and act as in ancient times. Rahab and the dragon are poetic images of chaos-monsters, here standing for Egypt, which God defeated at the Exodus.

f.g: A poetic name for a sea monster, used for Egypt.
Another chaos-monster image, also used of Pharaoh.

chapters.n: God dried the sea and made a path for the redeemed to cross — the Red Sea crossing.

f.w: made the depths of the sea a way for the ransomed to pass over

chapters.n: So the Lord’s redeemed will return to Zion with singing. The Book of Mormon adds “holiness” to the everlasting joy upon their heads. Sorrow will flee away.

f.w: the redeemed of the Lord shall return

chapters.n: God says, “I am he that comforteth you.” Why fear mortal men who wither like grass?

f.w: I am he that comforteth you

chapters.n: Why forget your Maker and live in constant fear of oppressors? Where is their fury now? It will vanish before God.
The captive in exile will soon be released, not left to die in a pit or go hungry.
“I am the Lord thy God, whose waves roared; the Lord of Hosts is my name.” The Book of Mormon omits the KJV phrase “that divided the sea.”

f.g: The Lord of the armies of heaven.

chapters.n: God has put His words in His people’s mouths and sheltered them in His hand, establishing them as His people.

f.w: I have put my words in thy mouth

chapters.n: Jerusalem is called to wake up. She has drunk the cup of God’s wrath down to the bitter dregs — a picture of the suffering that followed her sins.

f.g: The bitter sediment at the bottom of a cup.

chapters.n: None of Jerusalem’s children are left to guide her or take her hand.

Two “sons” come to her in her ruin. The KJV reads “two things” (desolation and destruction); the Book of Mormon’s “two sons” is often connected by Latter-day Saints to the two prophets of Revelation 11, who minister in Jerusalem in the last days.
Her other sons have fainted in the streets, caught like a wild antelope in a net, overwhelmed by God’s rebuke. The Book of Mormon adds “save these two.”

f.g: Hebrew te’o — likely an antelope or oryx.

chapters.n: Hear this, you who are afflicted and staggering — though not from wine.
The Lord pleads His people’s cause: He takes the cup of trembling from their hand. They will never drink it again.

f.w: pleadeth the cause of his people

chapters.n: Instead, He gives the cup to their oppressors, who had forced Israel to lie down like a road for them to walk on.

f.w: Bow down, that we may go over
f.g: Conquerors sometimes literally walked on the backs of the defeated.

chapters.n: Now Jacob quotes Isaiah 52:1. Zion is called to awake and put on her strength and beautiful garments; nothing unclean will enter her again. Latter-day revelation explains this strength as priesthood authority.

f.w: put on thy strength, O Zion

chapters.n: Isaiah 52:2: Jerusalem must shake off the dust, rise, and free herself from the chains on her neck. Latter-day revelation explains these chains as the curses of God, which scattered Israel can shake off by returning to Him.

f.w: loose thyself from the bands of thy neck

chapters.n: Jacob explains why he read Isaiah: so the Nephites would understand the Lord’s covenants with all Israel. This chapter is one of the greatest sermons on the Atonement in all scripture.

God has spoken through prophets for generations about the Jews being restored to His true church and fold, and gathered to their promised lands. Gathering is first spiritual — to Christ — then physical.

f.w: restored to the true church and fold of God

chapters.n: Jacob shares this so his people can rejoice and lift their heads because of the blessings promised to their children.
Many of the Nephites have studied the future. They know their bodies will die, yet in their bodies they will see God — a hope of resurrection echoing Job.

f.w: in our bodies we shall see God

chapters.n: Christ will show Himself in a body to the Jews at Jerusalem. The great Creator will allow Himself to become subject to mortals and die for all, so all may become subject to Him.

f.w: subject unto man in the flesh

chapters.n: Death came to all because of the Fall, which came through transgression and cut humanity off from God. So a power of resurrection is needed to fulfill the Creator’s merciful plan.

f.w: the merciful plan of the great Creator
cut off from the presence of the Lord

chapters.n: So the Atonement must be infinite. Otherwise our corrupt mortal bodies could never become incorruptible; the first judgment — death — would last forever, and our bodies would crumble in the earth never to rise.

f.w: corruption could not put on incorruption

chapters.n: Jacob exclaims at God’s wisdom, mercy, and grace. Without resurrection, our spirits would be subject forever to the devil, the angel who fell.

Our spirits would become like the devil, shut out from God with the father of lies. Satan deceived Adam and Eve, disguises himself as an angel of light, and stirs up secret combinations — conspiracies of murder and darkness.

f.w: transformeth himself nigh unto an angel of light

f.g: Secret conspiracies bound by oaths to gain power or wealth through crime.

chapters.n: How good God is to prepare an escape from the “awful monster” of death and hell — physical death of the body and spiritual death of the spirit.
Through the Holy One of Israel, physical death — the grave — will give up its dead.
Spiritual death — hell — will also give up its dead. Spirits and bodies will be reunited by the power of Christ’s resurrection.

f.w: the bodies and the spirits of men will be restored one to the other

chapters.n: Paradise will release the spirits of the righteous and the grave their bodies. All become immortal living souls, with perfect knowledge.
With perfect knowledge, the guilty will fully remember their guilt and uncleanness, while the righteous will fully know their joy and righteousness, clothed in a robe of purity.

f.w: perfect knowledge of all our guilt

chapters.n: Once resurrected and immortal, everyone must stand before the judgment-seat of the Holy One of Israel and be judged.

f.w: the judgment-seat of the Holy One of Israel

chapters.n: God’s unchanging word: the righteous remain righteous and the filthy remain filthy. The unrepentant share the fate of the devil, described as an endless lake of fire — an image of intense spiritual torment.

f.w: they who are filthy shall be filthy still
a lake of fire and brimstone
f.g: An image of the anguish of guilt; brimstone is sulfur.

chapters.n: God is great and just: He fulfills all His words, and His law must be satisfied.
The righteous — those who believed in Christ and bore the world’s crosses, ignoring its scorn — will inherit God’s kingdom with full and lasting joy.

f.w: endured the crosses of the world
prepared for them from the foundation of the world

chapters.n: God’s mercy rescues His saints from the devil, death, hell, and endless torment.

f.w: the greatness of the mercy of our God

chapters.n: God is holy and knows all things; nothing is hidden from Him.
Christ comes to save all who will listen to Him. He suffers the pains of every man, woman, and child in Adam’s family — the Atonement is deeply personal.

f.w: he suffereth the pains of all men

chapters.n: He suffers so that resurrection will come to everyone and all can stand before Him at judgment.

f.w: that the resurrection might pass upon all men

chapters.n: He commands everyone to repent, be baptized in His name, and have perfect faith in Him in order to be saved in His kingdom.

f.w: repent, and be baptized in his name

chapters.n: Those who will not repent, believe, be baptized, and endure to the end will be “damned” — stopped in their progress, unable to enter God’s presence.

f.g: Condemned; halted from progressing to God’s full presence.

chapters.n: Where there is no law given, there is no punishment or condemnation. Christ’s mercy covers those who never knew God’s law.

f.w: where there is no law given there is no punishment

chapters.n: The Atonement satisfies justice for those without the law — such as little children and those who never heard the gospel — restoring them to God. Latter-day Saints also teach that the gospel is preached to the dead.

f.w: all those who have not the law given to them

chapters.n: But woe to those who have all God’s commandments, as the Nephites do, and break them and waste their probation. Greater knowledge brings greater responsibility.

f.w: wasteth the days of his probation

chapters.n: Satan’s cunning plan exploits human pride. When people become educated, they may think they’re wise enough to ignore God’s counsel — and their wisdom becomes foolishness.

f.w: When they are learned they think they are wise

chapters.n: But education is good when people also follow God’s counsel. The problem is pride, not learning.
Woe to the worldly rich who despise the poor, persecute the meek, and make their treasure their god. Their treasure will perish with them.
Woe to those who refuse to hear — spiritually deaf.

f.w: the deaf that will not hear

chapters.n: Woe to those who refuse to see — spiritually blind.

f.w: the blind that will not see

chapters.n: Woe to the “uncircumcised of heart” — those whose hearts are not dedicated to God. Their sins will strike them at the last day.

f.g: Not inwardly committed to God’s covenant, whatever outward signs they bear.

chapters.n: Woe to the liar.
Woe to the deliberate murderer.
Woe to those who commit sexual sin.

f.g: Sexual immorality.

chapters.n: Woe to idol worshipers — the devil delights in them.
Woe to all who die in their sins: they will return to God, see His face, and still be in their sins.
Remember how serious it is to sin against God and yield to the devil. To be carnally minded — focused on worldly appetites — is death; to be spiritually minded is eternal life.
Jacob asks them not to call his words harsh — that would be rejecting truth. Truth is hard on uncleanness, but the righteous don’t fear it because they love it.
Come to the Lord. The way is narrow but straight, and the gatekeeper is Christ Himself. He employs no servant at the gate and cannot be deceived — there is no other way in.

f.w: the keeper of the gate is the Holy One of Israel

chapters.n: He opens to all who knock. But those puffed up by learning, wisdom, or riches must cast aside their pride and humble themselves before Him, or He will not open.

f.w: whoso knocketh, to him will he open

chapters.n: Otherwise the happiness prepared for the saints will remain hidden from the proud forever.
Jacob symbolically shakes his garments, showing that he has done his duty to warn them. Having taught them, he is free of responsibility for their sins.

f.w: I take off my garments, and I shake them before you

f.g: Free of responsibility for their sins, having warned them.

chapters.n: Turn from your sins, shake off the devil’s chains, and come to God, the rock of your salvation.
Prepare for Judgment Day so you won’t shrink in fear, perfectly remembering your guilt and admitting the devil has captured you.
Jacob asks: would he need to stir them up so strongly if they were pure?

f.g: To tear up, as a harrow breaks up soil — to distress deeply.

chapters.n: If they were holy, he would speak of holiness. Because they are not, he must teach the consequences of sin.
Jacob’s own heart hates sin and loves righteousness; he will praise God’s holy name.
Quoting Isaiah 55:1, Jacob invites the thirsty to come to the waters and “buy” without money — salvation is a free gift.
Don’t spend your money or labor on what can’t satisfy. Come to Christ and feast on what never perishes, and let your soul delight in “fatness” — abundance.

f.g: Richness, abundance — the best part of a feast.

chapters.n: Remember God’s words, pray continually day and night, give thanks, and rejoice.
Jacob marvels at God’s covenants and condescension. Because of His grace, the Nephites’ descendants will not be completely destroyed and will one day become a righteous branch of Israel.
Jacob ends for the day, promising to continue tomorrow (chapter 10).
The next day Jacob continues speaking about the “righteous branch” — the future descendants of the Nephites.
Many of their descendants will perish because of unbelief, but God will be merciful to many, restoring them to the knowledge of their Redeemer.

f.w: the true knowledge of their Redeemer

chapters.n: An angel told Jacob that the Redeemer’s name would be Christ, the first time the title appears in the Book of Mormon. Jacob speaks of the wickedness of the leaders and people who would reject Him in that generation; the Book of Mormon elsewhere urges gratitude and love toward the Jews.

f.g: Greek Christos, “Anointed One” — the same meaning as Hebrew Messiah.

chapters.n: If such miracles were done among other nations, Jacob says, they would repent and recognize Him as God.
Because of priestcraft — religious leaders seeking gain and praise — and iniquity, people at Jerusalem would harden themselves against Him and have Him crucified.

f.g: Preaching for personal gain and popularity rather than for God.

chapters.n: Destruction, famine, disease, and bloodshed would follow, and survivors would be scattered among the nations.
But when they believe that Jesus is the Christ, God will keep His covenant to restore them physically to their promised lands.

f.w: they shall be restored in the flesh

chapters.n: They will be gathered from their long dispersion across the earth, and Gentile nations will be honored for helping them return.
Gentile kings and queens will care for them like nursing parents, fulfilling Isaiah. God’s promises to the Gentiles are great.
This land (the Americas) will be the Nephites’ inheritance, and the Gentiles too will be blessed here.
It will be a land of liberty for the Gentiles, with no kings ruling over them.

f.w: there shall be no kings upon the land

chapters.n: God will protect this land against all other nations.

f.g: Strengthen and protect.

chapters.n: Whoever fights against Zion will perish.
Anyone who sets up a king against God will perish, for the Lord, the King of heaven, will be their King and their light.

f.w: I, the Lord, the king of heaven, will be their king

chapters.n: To fulfill His covenants, God must destroy secret works of darkness, murder, and abomination — the secret combinations that threaten free peoples.
Whoever fights Zion — Jew or Gentile, slave or free, male or female — belongs to the “whore of all the earth.” Those not for God are against Him.

f.w: they who are not for me are against me

chapters.n: God will fulfill all He has promised to do for people in mortality.
God will afflict Lehi’s descendants through the Gentiles, yet soften Gentile hearts to become like fathers to them. Gentiles who accept the covenant will be counted as Israel.

f.w: numbered among the house of Israel

chapters.n: God dedicates this choice land forever to Lehi’s descendants and those counted with them, and He wants all who live here to worship Him.
With such knowledge, Jacob says, remember God, set aside sin, and don’t hang your heads — we are not cast off. We were driven from our homeland but led to a better one, an “isle of the sea.”

f.g: In biblical usage, any land reached by sea, even a continent.

chapters.n: Since Isaiah speaks of “isles” (plural), there must be other lands with other scattered Israelites as well.

f.w: there must needs be more than this

chapters.n: God has led groups away from Israel at various times, and He remembers all who have been broken off — including the Nephites.

f.w: the Lord remembereth all them who have been broken off

chapters.n: Cheer up, Jacob says — you are free to choose everlasting death or eternal life.
Reconcile yourselves to God’s will rather than the devil’s and the flesh’s. And remember: even after you are reconciled, it is only through God’s grace that you are saved.

f.w: reconcile yourselves to the will of God
only in and through the grace of God that ye are saved

chapters.n: Jacob prays that God will raise them from physical death through the Resurrection and from spiritual death through the Atonement, so they can praise Him by grace in His eternal kingdom.
Nephi takes over again. Jacob said much more, but Nephi recorded only what he felt was enough.

f.g: Is enough for my purposes.

chapters.n: Nephi introduces thirteen chapters of Isaiah. He loves Isaiah’s words and will apply them to his people, because Isaiah saw the Redeemer just as Nephi did.

f.w: I will liken his words unto my people

chapters.n: Jacob also saw Christ. Isaiah, Nephi, and Jacob are three witnesses, and God establishes His word through multiple witnesses.
Nephi delights in proving that Christ will come. The law of Moses and everything God has given since the beginning “typify” Him — they are symbols pointing to Christ.

f.g: Serving as a type — a symbol or foreshadowing.

chapters.n: He delights in God’s covenants, grace, justice, power, and mercy in the eternal plan of deliverance from death.

f.w: the great and eternal plan of deliverance

chapters.n: He delights in teaching that without Christ, all would perish.

f.w: save Christ should come all men must perish

chapters.n: If there were no Christ, there would be no God and no creation. But there is a God, and He is Christ, who will come at His appointed time. Nephi identifies the God of Israel with Christ.

f.w: there is a God, and he is Christ

chapters.n: Nephi now quotes Isaiah so his people may rejoice for all humanity. He invites readers to liken Isaiah’s words to themselves and all people.

Nephi begins quoting Isaiah 2–14 (2 Nephi 12–24). Isaiah, son of Amoz, prophesied in Jerusalem about 740–700 BC, during the rise of Assyria. This heading introduces a vision about Judah and Jerusalem.

In the last days, the “mountain of the Lord’s house” — His temple — will be raised above all hills, and all nations will stream to it. Latter-day Saints see fulfillment in temples, including those in the Rocky Mountains, and in a future temple in Jerusalem.

f.w: the mountain of the Lord's house

chapters.n: People will invite each other to go up to God’s house to learn His ways. His law will go out from Zion and His word from Jerusalem — two centers of God’s work.

f.w: he will teach us of his ways
out of Zion shall go forth the law

chapters.n: The Lord will judge the nations. Weapons will be turned into farm tools, and war will end — the peace of the Millennium.

f.w: they shall beat their swords into plow-shares

f.g: Curved blades for trimming vines.

chapters.n: Isaiah calls Israel to walk in the Lord’s light. The Book of Mormon adds, “yea, come, for ye have all gone astray, every one to his wicked ways” — not in the KJV.
Isaiah turns to Judah’s sins: they have filled up with foreign eastern practices and follow fortune-tellers like the Philistines, embracing foreign ways and alliances.

f.g: Fortune-tellers who claim to predict the future.

f.w: please themselves in the children of strangers
f.g: Make deals or alliances with foreigners.

chapters.n: The land is full of silver, gold, horses, and chariots. Israel’s kings were warned not to multiply these, since trust in wealth and military power replaces trust in God.
The land is also full of idols. People worship what their own hands have made.

f.w: they worship the work of their own hands

chapters.n: The Book of Mormon reads that neither the lowly (“mean man”) nor the great humble themselves — the KJV says they do bow down (to idols). Either way, pride and idolatry prevent forgiveness.

f.g: Common, ordinary person (not “cruel”).

chapters.n: The wicked will try to hide in rocks and dust from the terror of the Lord’s glory. The Book of Mormon adds “O ye wicked ones.”
Human pride will be humbled, and the Lord alone will be exalted in that day.

f.w: the Lord alone shall be exalted

chapters.n: The day of the Lord is coming upon all nations and every proud person. The Book of Mormon expands this verse, stressing that it will come soon and on everyone.

f.w: the day of the Lord of Hosts

chapters.n: It will come upon the tall cedars of Lebanon and oaks of Bashan — famous majestic trees symbolizing proud people and nations.

f.g: Prized tall trees used in Solomon’s temple.
A fertile region east of the Sea of Galilee, known for oaks and cattle.

chapters.n: It will come upon high mountains and hills, and — the Book of Mormon adds — upon proud nations and every people.
Every high tower and fortified wall — symbols of human security — will be brought low.

f.g: Fortified wall.

chapters.n: The day of the Lord will also humble trading ships and their luxuries. Scholars have noticed that the Book of Mormon includes both “ships of the sea” (found in the ancient Greek Septuagint) and “ships of Tarshish” (in the Hebrew), as if preserving a fuller original line.

f.g: Large merchant ships for long voyages; Tarshish was a distant trading port, perhaps in Spain.
Desirable objects or luxury goods.

chapters.n: Human pride will be bowed down, and the Lord alone will be exalted — a refrain repeated from verse 11.

f.g: Arrogant pride.

chapters.n: God will completely abolish idols.

f.w: the idols he shall utterly abolish

chapters.n: People will flee into caves when the Lord rises to shake the earth — imagery associated with the Second Coming.
People will throw their silver and gold idols to the moles and bats — leaving them in dark holes, seeing their worthlessness at last.

f.w: to the moles and to the bats
f.g: Into dark, forgotten places.

chapters.n: They will hide in the clefts of rugged rocks when the Lord shakes the earth.

f.g: Cracks or crevices.

chapters.n: Stop trusting in mortal man, whose life is only a breath. What is he really worth compared to God?

f.w: whose breath is in his nostrils

chapters.n: Isaiah 3 warns that the Lord will take away Judah’s support — its “stay and staff,” meaning its food, water, and leaders. This came true during sieges by Assyria and Babylon.

f.g: Support and supply; everything they lean on.

chapters.n: He will remove warriors, judges, prophets, wise men, and elders — the people society depends on.

f.g: The elder; experienced leaders.

chapters.n: Military captains, nobles, counselors, skilled craftsmen, and gifted speakers will also be removed. Babylon later deported exactly these kinds of people.

f.g: A military officer over fifty soldiers.
Skilled craftsman.
Possibly “skilled enchanter” in Hebrew.

chapters.n: With capable leaders gone, immature and inexperienced people — “children” — will rule.
Society will break down: neighbors oppress neighbors, the young defy the old, and the lowly insult the honorable.

f.g: The disreputable against the respected.

chapters.n: Things get so bad that a man will beg his relative to lead simply because he owns a cloak.

f.w: Thou hast clothing, be thou our ruler
f.g: Even minimal resources seem like qualifications to lead.

chapters.n: The relative will refuse: he can’t heal the nation’s wounds, for he has no food or clothing either.

f.w: I will not be a healer
f.g: Hebrew: “binder of wounds.”

chapters.n: Jerusalem and Judah collapse because their words and actions defy the Lord.

f.w: to provoke the eyes of his glory
f.g: To openly defy God in His very presence.

chapters.n: Their faces show their guilt. Like Sodom, they don’t even hide their sin. In harming others, they have really harmed themselves.

f.w: they have rewarded evil unto themselves

chapters.n: Tell the righteous it will go well with them — they will enjoy the fruits of their good deeds.

f.w: they shall eat the fruit of their doings

chapters.n: Woe to the wicked; they will receive what their own hands have done.
God laments that His people are oppressed by immature leaders and misled by those who should guide them.

f.w: they who lead thee cause thee to err

chapters.n: The Lord rises like a judge in a courtroom to plead His case against the people.

f.w: The Lord standeth up to plead

chapters.n: He brings charges against Judah’s elders and princes: they have devoured the vineyard (God’s people) and stored the plunder taken from the poor in their houses.

f.w: ye have eaten up the vineyard

chapters.n: “What do you mean by crushing my people and grinding the faces of the poor?” God takes oppression of the poor personally.

f.w: grind the faces of the poor

chapters.n: Isaiah now condemns the proud “daughters of Zion,” the wealthy women of Jerusalem, who strut with raised necks, flirtatious eyes, and jingling ankle ornaments. Their vanity symbolizes the whole nation’s pride.

f.g: Seductive, flirtatious glances.
Walking with small, affected steps.

chapters.n: Their pride will be replaced with disease and humiliation — the fate of captives in war.

f.g: Scalp disease, perhaps causing baldness.
Uncover, expose.

chapters.n: Isaiah lists the finery that will be stripped away: anklets, hairnets, and crescent-shaped ornaments.

f.g: Splendor, finery.
Hairnets or headbands.
Crescent-shaped ornaments.

chapters.n: Necklaces, bracelets, and veils.

f.g: Veils or scarves.

chapters.n: Headdresses, ankle chains, sashes, perfume boxes, and charms.

f.g: Probably perfume boxes or vials.
Possibly amulets or charms.

chapters.n: Rings and nose rings.
Festive robes, cloaks, shawls, and purses.

f.g: Shawls or wraps.
Purses or bags (KJV guessed hair-curling pins).

chapters.n: Mirrors, fine linen, turbans, and veils. The long list shows how much they had invested in appearance.

f.g: Hand mirrors of polished metal.

chapters.n: Every symbol of luxury will be reversed: perfume to stench, sash to rope, styled hair to baldness, fine robes to sackcloth, and beauty to branding — the treatment of captives.

f.g: A rich robe or ornamented garment.
Possibly branding, a mark of slavery.

chapters.n: Jerusalem’s men will die in battle.

f.w: Thy men shall fall by the sword

chapters.n: Jerusalem is pictured as a widow sitting on the ground at her gates, mourning and empty — a scene fulfilled when Babylon destroyed the city.

So many men will die in war that seven women will beg one man to marry them, offering to provide their own food and clothes, just to avoid the shame of being unmarried and childless. This continues the judgment of Isaiah 3.

f.g: To remove the social disgrace of being unmarried or childless.

chapters.n: But then hope: the “branch of the Lord” will be beautiful and glorious for the survivors of Israel. Many see the Branch as a title for the Messiah.

f.g: Attractive, lovely.

chapters.n: Those who remain in Zion and Jerusalem will be called holy — everyone whose name is recorded among the living.
This will happen after the Lord washes away Zion’s filth and Jerusalem’s bloodguilt by a spirit of judgment and burning — purification by fire.
God will place a cloud by day and fire by night over every home and gathering in Zion, like the pillar that guided Israel in the Exodus. His glory will be their protection.

f.w: a cloud and smoke by day and the shining of a flaming fire by night

chapters.n: A tabernacle — a shelter — will give shade from the heat and refuge from storm. Latter-day Saints often apply this to the safety found in Zion and its stakes.

f.g: Shelter, hiding place.

chapters.n: Isaiah 5 opens with a song about a vineyard on a fertile hill. The “beloved” who owns it is God.

f.g: The Lord, as owner of the vineyard.
Hebrew: “a horn, son of oil” — a rich slope.

chapters.n: He did everything for his vineyard: fenced it, cleared stones, planted the best vines, built a watchtower and a winepress. But it produced only wild, sour grapes.

f.g: Small, bitter, worthless grapes.

chapters.n: God asks the people of Jerusalem and Judah to judge between Him and His vineyard.
What more could He have done? Yet it produced only wild grapes. Compare the Lord’s lament in Zenos’s allegory of the olive tree.

f.w: What could have been done more to my vineyard

chapters.n: So He will remove its hedge and wall, letting animals trample and eat it.

f.g: Come now; an expression to get attention.

chapters.n: He will leave it unpruned and untilled, overgrown with briers and thorns, and command the clouds to withhold rain.

The meaning: the vineyard is Israel, and Judah is His favored plant. He looked for justice (mishpat) but found bloodshed (mispach); for righteousness (tsedaqah) but heard a cry (tse‘aqah). Isaiah uses a Hebrew wordplay.

f.w: he looked for judgment, and behold, oppression
f.g: A pun in Hebrew: mishpat (justice) vs. mispach (bloodshed).

chapters.n: The first of six woes: against land-grabbers who buy up house after house and field after field until they live alone, pushing out the poor.
God warns that many grand houses will be left empty and cities deserted.

f.g: Empty, ruined.

chapters.n: Harvests will fail badly: ten acres of vines will produce only about six gallons of wine, and planted seed will return only a tenth of itself.

f.g: A liquid measure of about 6 gallons (22 liters).
A dry measure, about 6 bushels; an ephah is one-tenth of a homer.

chapters.n: Woe to those who start drinking early and party into the night.

f.g: Beer or other intoxicating drink.

chapters.n: Their feasts have music and wine, but they give no thought to what the Lord is doing.

f.g: A harp-like stringed instrument.
A small drum or tambourine.

chapters.n: So the people go into captivity “because they have no knowledge” — they ignored God. Their nobles starve and the crowds die of thirst.
The grave (Sheol) opens its mouth wide to swallow the proud and partying multitudes.

f.g: Hebrew Sheol — the grave or world of the dead.

chapters.n: Both lowly and mighty will be humbled, and the proud brought low.

f.g: The ordinary person.

chapters.n: But the Lord will be exalted through His just judgment and shown holy through righteousness.

f.g: Shown to be holy.

chapters.n: Lambs will graze in the ruins of the rich, and strangers will eat in the deserted estates.

f.g: The wealthy.

chapters.n: Woe to those who drag their sins behind them like a cart pulled with ropes — tied to their wrongdoing.

f.g: Ropes of falsehood or emptiness.

chapters.n: They mock God: “Let Him hurry up and do His work so we can see it!” — taunting His warnings.
Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who swap darkness for light and bitter for sweet. Moral confusion is a mark of a decaying society.

f.w: call evil good, and good evil

chapters.n: Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes.
Woe to those whose only heroism is in drinking and mixing strong drink.

f.g: Champions at drinking — sarcasm.

chapters.n: They take bribes to declare the guilty innocent and deny justice to the innocent.
Like stubble in fire, their roots will rot and their blossoms blow away as dust, because they rejected God’s law and word.

f.w: as the fire devoureth the stubble

chapters.n: God’s anger strikes His people; hills tremble and bodies lie in the streets. Yet “his hand is stretched out still” — a refrain repeated in Isaiah 9–10. It can describe continuing judgment, and Latter-day Saints also see in it God’s outstretched hand of mercy.

f.w: his hand is stretched out still

chapters.n: God will raise a banner to distant nations and whistle for them to come quickly. Historically this meant Assyria’s armies; Latter-day Saints also see the latter-day gathering to Christ’s ensign.

f.g: A banner or flag raised as a rallying point.
Whistle as a signal.

chapters.n: They will come tireless and alert, belts fastened and sandal straps unbroken — ready and unstoppable.

f.g: Belt; tightening it meant being ready for action.
Sandal strap.

chapters.n: Their arrows are sharp and bows strung; horses’ hooves are hard as flint and chariot wheels spin like a whirlwind. Some readers see hints of modern transportation in this imagery.

f.g: Swift chariots.

chapters.n: They roar like young lions, seize their prey, and carry it off with none to rescue it.
Their roar will be like the sea’s; the land will be covered in darkness and sorrow, and the sky’s light will grow dark.

Isaiah 6 records Isaiah’s call. In the year King Uzziah died (around 740 BC), Isaiah saw the Lord on a lofty throne, His robe filling the temple. Nephi says Isaiah saw his Redeemer; John 12:41 also says Isaiah saw Christ’s glory.

f.g: The trailing hem of his robe.

chapters.n: Seraphim — heavenly beings whose name means “burning ones” — stand above Him. With two wings they cover their faces in reverence, with two their feet in humility, and with two they fly.

f.g: Hebrew “burning ones” — angelic beings in God’s presence.
Two.

chapters.n: They call to each other: “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of Hosts.” Repeating a word three times is Hebrew’s strongest way to say “most holy.” His glory fills the whole earth.
The doorposts shake at their voice, and the temple fills with smoke — signs of God’s presence, as at Sinai.

f.w: the house was filled with smoke

chapters.n: Isaiah cries “Woe is me! I am undone!” Seeing God’s holiness makes him painfully aware of his own impurity and his people’s.

f.g: I am ruined, lost.

chapters.n: A seraph flies to him holding a live coal taken with tongs from the altar.

f.g: A glowing coal from the temple altar — a symbol of cleansing fire.

chapters.n: The seraph touches Isaiah’s lips with the coal: his guilt is removed and his sin purged. Cleansing comes from the altar of sacrifice — a symbol pointing to Christ’s Atonement.

f.g: Atoned for, cleansed.

chapters.n: The Lord asks, “Whom shall I send?” Isaiah answers, “Here am I; send me.” The same words recall Christ’s offer in the premortal council.
Isaiah’s message will be rejected. The KJV reads as a command (“understand not”); the Book of Mormon reads “they understood not,” describing the people’s own refusal to understand.

f.g: KJV Isaiah 6:9 reads “but understand not.”

chapters.n: Isaiah’s preaching will make the people’s hearts “fat” (insensitive), their ears dull, and their eyes shut, because they refuse it. Truth rejected hardens the heart.

f.w: Make the heart of this people fat
f.g: Dull, unresponsive — Hebrew idiom for insensitivity.

chapters.n: “How long, Lord?” Until the cities are empty and the land desolate — fulfilled through the Assyrian and Babylonian invasions.
The Lord will remove the people far away, leaving the land abandoned — exile.

f.g: Widespread abandonment of the land.

chapters.n: Yet a tenth will remain. Like a felled terebinth or oak that still has life in its stump, a “holy seed” will survive and grow again — the remnant of Israel.

f.g: The terebinth, a large tree that can resprout from its stump.

chapters.n: Isaiah 7 is set around 735 BC. King Rezin of Syria (Aram) and King Pekah of Israel (the northern kingdom) march against Jerusalem to force Judah’s King Ahaz into their alliance against Assyria. They fail to take the city.
When the royal house of David hears that Syria has allied with Ephraim (Israel), Ahaz and his people tremble like trees in the wind.

f.g: The leading tribe of the northern kingdom; a name for the kingdom of Israel.
Allied.

chapters.n: God sends Isaiah with his son Shearjashub to meet Ahaz at the water channel, where the king was likely inspecting Jerusalem’s water supply for a siege. The son’s name means “a remnant shall return” — a living message.

f.g: Hebrew “a remnant shall return.”
Where cloth was washed and bleached.

chapters.n: Isaiah’s message: stay calm and don’t fear. These two kings are just smoldering stumps of firewood — mostly burned out.

f.g: Burnt-out sticks, still smoking but nearly spent.

chapters.n: Syria, Ephraim, and Pekah have plotted against Judah.

f.g: Pekah, king of Israel — named by his father’s name, perhaps with contempt.

chapters.n: Their plan was to attack Judah, break in, and install a puppet king, “the son of Tabeal.”

f.g: An otherwise unknown candidate for a puppet king.
Harass, terrify.

chapters.n: God declares: their plan will not succeed.
These kingdoms are merely human. Within sixty-five years Ephraim will be shattered as a people. Assyria conquered Israel in 722 BC and resettled the land with foreigners over the following decades.

f.g: Sixty-five years.

chapters.n: Samaria is Israel’s capital and Pekah its head. Then the key line: “If you will not believe, you will not be established” — a Hebrew wordplay on faith (’aman) and firmness.

f.w: If ye will not believe surely ye shall not be established

chapters.n: The Lord speaks again to Ahaz.
God offers Ahaz any sign he wants, from the depths to the heights.
Ahaz refuses, pretending piety: “I won’t test the Lord.” In truth he had already decided to seek Assyria’s help rather than trust God.

f.w: neither will I tempt the Lord

chapters.n: Isaiah rebukes the house of David: is it not enough to try people’s patience — must you try God’s too?

So the Lord gives a sign anyway: a virgin (or young woman) will conceive and bear a son named Immanuel, “God with us.” It had meaning for Ahaz’s day, and Matthew identifies its full fulfillment in Jesus’ birth to the virgin Mary.

f.g: Hebrew “God with us.”

chapters.n: The child will eat curds and honey — simple food in a land emptied by war — when he is old enough to know right from wrong.

f.g: Curds (thickened milk) and wild honey.

chapters.n: Before the child is old enough to choose right from wrong, the lands of the two kings Ahaz fears will be abandoned. Within a few years Assyria crushed both Syria and Israel.
But because Ahaz trusted Assyria rather than God, the Lord will bring Assyria’s king upon Judah — the worst days since the kingdom split.

f.w: the day that Ephraim departed from Judah

chapters.n: God will whistle for the “fly” of Egypt and the “bee” of Assyria — swarming armies from both great powers.

f.g: Whistle as a signal.

chapters.n: These armies will settle everywhere — valleys, caves, thorns, and bushes. No place will be untouched.
God will use Assyria, the “hired razor” from beyond the Euphrates, to shave Judah’s head, body hair, and beard — a picture of total humiliation, as captives were shaved.

f.g: Assyria, whom Ahaz had paid for help, becomes God’s tool against him.
Beyond the Euphrates — Assyria.

chapters.n: Survivors will live simply, each tending only a young cow and two sheep.
With so few people, the milk will be plentiful; survivors will eat curds and honey, the food of a depopulated land.
Valuable vineyards, once worth a thousand silver pieces, will become thorns and briers.

f.g: Silver coins or shekels.

chapters.n: The overgrown land will be fit only for hunting with bow and arrow.
Hillsides once carefully hoed will be left to grazing oxen and sheep.

f.g: A digging tool like a pickaxe or hoe.
Sheep and goats.

chapters.n: Isaiah 8: God tells Isaiah to write in large, plain letters the name “Maher-shalal-hash-baz,” meaning “swift to plunder, quick to spoil” — a warning that Assyria would soon loot Syria and Israel.

f.g: Hebrew “quick to the plunder, swift to the spoil.”
A large tablet or scroll.

chapters.n: Isaiah has two reliable witnesses confirm the writing, so when the prophecy comes true, no one can deny it was given beforehand.
Isaiah’s wife, called “the prophetess,” bears a son, and God tells them to give him this prophetic name.

f.g: Isaiah’s wife; perhaps a prophet in her own right.

chapters.n: Before the baby can say “Daddy” or “Mommy,” Assyria will plunder Damascus and Samaria. This was fulfilled around 732 BC, when Assyria took Damascus.
The Lord speaks to Isaiah again.
The people reject the gentle waters of Shiloah — Jerusalem’s quiet water supply, symbolizing God’s calm care — and admire the kings of Syria and Israel instead.

f.g: A gently flowing channel supplying Jerusalem; compare the later pool of Siloam.

chapters.n: So God will bring the mighty river — the king of Assyria — flooding over its banks. Rejecting quiet waters brings a flood.

f.g: The Euphrates, symbolizing Assyria’s power.

chapters.n: Assyria will sweep through Judah up to the neck — nearly drowning it, but not completely (Jerusalem survived in 701 BC). Its spreading wings cover “thy land, O Immanuel.”

f.w: he shall reach even to the neck

chapters.n: Isaiah taunts the nations: band together, arm yourselves — you will still be shattered.

f.g: Prepare for battle by fastening your belts.

chapters.n: Make plans — they will fail; give orders — they won’t stand, “for God is with us” (Immanuel).

f.g: Hebrew ‘immanu ’el — the meaning of Immanuel.

chapters.n: With a firm hand, God warned Isaiah not to follow the people’s way of thinking.

f.g: With compelling power.

chapters.n: Don’t call everything a conspiracy as the people do, and don’t share their fears.

f.g: A conspiracy or alliance.

chapters.n: Instead, treat the Lord as holy; let Him be the one you fear and revere.

f.w: Sanctify the Lord of Hosts himself

chapters.n: For those who trust Him, the Lord is a sanctuary. For those who don’t, He becomes a stumbling stone and a trap. The New Testament applies this to Christ.

f.g: A trap or snare.

chapters.n: Many will stumble, fall, be broken, snared, and captured.
Isaiah tells his followers to bind up and seal his testimony and teaching, preserving it for the future.
Isaiah will wait for the Lord, even while He hides His face from Israel.

f.w: I will wait upon the Lord

chapters.n: Isaiah and his sons, with their symbolic names (Isaiah = “the Lord saves”), are living signs from God.

f.w: I and the children whom the Lord hath given me

chapters.n: When people tell you to consult mediums and spiritists who whisper and mutter, ask: shouldn’t people seek their God? The Book of Mormon reads “for the living to hear from the dead?” — a slightly clearer question than the KJV.

f.g: Spirits of the dead supposedly contacted by mediums.
Chirp and whisper — the sounds of spiritist practices.

chapters.n: Turn to God’s law and testimony. Anyone who speaks contrary to it has no light.

f.w: To the law and to the testimony

chapters.n: Those who reject God will wander distressed and hungry, then curse their king and God as they look upward.

f.g: Severely distressed.
Become enraged.

chapters.n: Looking around they will see only trouble, darkness, and anguish, and be thrust into deep gloom. The next chapter answers this darkness with a great light.

Isaiah 9 begins with hope after the darkness of chapter 8. The northern regions of Zebulun and Naphtali (around Galilee) were the first to suffer Assyrian invasion, but their gloom will not last. The Book of Mormon reads “the Red Sea” where the KJV has “the sea” — a puzzling difference scholars still discuss.

f.g: Galilee, a region with many non-Israelites.

chapters.n: The people walking in darkness have seen a great light. Matthew applies this to Jesus beginning His ministry in Galilee — the very region first darkened by conquest.

God has multiplied the nation and increased its joy — like the joy of harvest or of dividing the spoils of victory. The Book of Mormon reads “increased the joy,” where the KJV text says “not increased the joy,” matching what many translators now prefer.

f.w: according to the joy in harvest

chapters.n: God has broken the oppressor’s yoke and rod, as He did in Gideon’s victory over Midian.
Warriors’ boots and blood-soaked garments will be burned as fuel — the end of war itself.

One of the most beloved messianic prophecies: a child born, a son given, who will govern. His titles — Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace — declare His divine nature. Latter-day Saints see Him as Jesus Christ.

f.w: unto us a child is born

f.g: Christ is “Father” as Creator and as the father of those born again through Him.

chapters.n: His government and peace will grow without end on David’s throne, established in justice forever. The Lord’s own zeal will accomplish it.
Now Isaiah returns to the northern kingdom: the Lord has sent His word against Jacob/Israel.

f.g: It has fallen upon Israel.

chapters.n: All will know it, including Ephraim and Samaria, who speak in pride and stubbornness.

f.g: Arrogant stubbornness.

chapters.n: Their boast: “The bricks fell? We’ll rebuild with cut stone. The sycamores were cut down? We’ll plant cedars.” They treat God’s warnings as a chance to build bigger, refusing to repent.

f.g: Common fig-mulberry trees used for cheap lumber, vs. costly cedar.

chapters.n: So the Lord will raise Rezin’s enemies against Israel and join their foes together.

f.g: Assyria and others opposed to Syria’s king.

chapters.n: Syria from the east and Philistines from the west will devour Israel. The refrain returns: His anger is not turned away; His hand is still stretched out.

f.w: his hand is stretched out still

chapters.n: Even after being struck, the people do not turn to the God who disciplines them.

f.w: turneth not unto him that smiteth them

chapters.n: So God will cut off head and tail, palm branch and reed — high and low — in a single day.

f.g: Palm branch (the top) and reed (the bottom) — the high and the lowly.

chapters.n: The “head” is the elders and nobles; the “tail” is false prophets who teach lies.
The leaders mislead the people, and those who follow them are destroyed.

f.w: the leaders of this people cause them to err

chapters.n: Even the young men, orphans, and widows — usually objects of God’s compassion — will share in the judgment, because hypocrisy and wickedness have spread to all. The refrain repeats.

f.g: Folly here means moral wickedness, not just foolishness.

chapters.n: Wickedness itself burns like a wildfire, consuming briers, thorns, and thickets until smoke rises in columns. Sin destroys from within.
Through God’s wrath the land is scorched. The people become fuel, and no one spares even his brother.

f.w: no man shall spare his brother

chapters.n: Starving and never satisfied, they consume one another — even their own kin. Civil strife eats the nation alive.

f.w: the flesh of his own arm
