f.g: Their own kin and allies.

chapters.n: Manasseh and Ephraim, brother tribes, fight each other, and together turn against Judah. Still His anger is not turned away; His hand is stretched out still.

f.g: The two tribes descended from Joseph.

chapters.n: Isaiah 10 begins with woe to lawmakers who write unjust laws and oppressive decrees.

f.g: Oppression, trouble.

chapters.n: Their laws deny justice to the needy, steal the rights of the poor, and prey on widows and orphans — the very people God commands His people to protect.

f.w: that widows may be their prey

chapters.n: What will they do on the day of reckoning when disaster comes from afar? Where will they run, and where will they leave their wealth?

f.g: The day of God’s judgment.

chapters.n: They will cower among the prisoners or fall among the dead. The refrain sounds a last time: His hand is still stretched out.

f.w: his hand is stretched out still

chapters.n: God addresses Assyria as the rod of His anger — the tool He uses to discipline His people.

f.w: O Assyrian, the rod of mine anger

chapters.n: God sends Assyria against godless Judah/Israel to plunder and trample them like mud in the streets.

f.g: Here, a godless or profane nation.

chapters.n: But Assyria doesn’t see itself as God’s tool. Its goal is simply to destroy and conquer many nations.

f.g: However.

chapters.n: Assyria’s king boasts: “Aren’t my commanders all kings?” His vassals are greater than other nations’ rulers.
He lists cities he conquered: Calno, Carchemish, Hamath, Arpad, Samaria, Damascus. Each fell like the others — so why would Jerusalem be different?

f.g: A major city on the Euphrates, taken by Assyria in 717 BC.

chapters.n: He has conquered kingdoms whose idols were greater than those of Jerusalem and Samaria.
Since he destroyed Samaria and its idols, why not Jerusalem? He wrongly counts the Lord as just another idol.
When God has finished His disciplinary work on Zion and Jerusalem, He will punish the Assyrian king’s arrogant heart and proud looks.

f.w: the stout heart of the king of Assyria

chapters.n: The king brags that he did it all by his own strength and wisdom: moving borders, seizing treasures, and toppling rulers.

f.w: By the strength of my hand

chapters.n: He boasts he gathered nations’ wealth like eggs from an unguarded nest — no one flapped a wing or chirped.

f.g: Easily, without resistance.

chapters.n: Can an axe boast against the one who swings it? Assyria is only a tool in God’s hand, yet acts as though it were the one in charge.
So God will send wasting disease among Assyria’s strong warriors and a fire beneath its glory.

f.g: Wasting sickness among the sturdy warriors.

chapters.n: Israel’s Light — the Holy One — will become a fire that burns up Assyria’s thorns and briers in one day.

f.w: the light of Israel shall be for a fire

chapters.n: It will consume the glory of Assyria’s forest and fields, body and soul — they will waste away like a sick man (or a fainting standard-bearer).

f.g: Possibly “as when a sick man wastes away.”

chapters.n: So few trees will remain that a child could count them — Assyria’s army will be decimated.

f.w: that a child may write them
f.g: So few a child could list them.

chapters.n: In that day, Israel’s remnant will no longer lean on the nation that struck them (as Ahaz leaned on Assyria) but will rely truly on the Holy One of Israel.

f.g: Lean on, rely on.

chapters.n: “A remnant shall return” — the meaning of the name of Isaiah’s son Shearjashub — to the Mighty God.
Though Israel be as numerous as sand, only a remnant will return. The destruction decreed will overflow with righteousness — justice that leads to a purified people.

f.w: a remnant of them shall return

f.g: Complete destruction.

chapters.n: The Lord will carry out the decreed destruction throughout the land.
God comforts His people in Zion: don’t fear Assyria, even though it strikes you as Egypt once did.

f.w: be not afraid of the Assyrian

chapters.n: In a very short time God’s anger against Judah will end and turn to Assyria’s destruction.
God will lash Assyria as He struck Midian at the rock of Oreb in Gideon’s day, and lift His rod as He did over the Red Sea against Egypt.

f.w: as his rod was upon the sea

chapters.n: Assyria’s burden and yoke will be lifted from Judah’s neck and broken “because of the anointing” — through God’s anointed one. Many see a pointer to the Messiah, the Anointed.

f.g: Possibly “because of fatness” in Hebrew; often read as pointing to the Anointed One.

chapters.n: Isaiah pictures the Assyrian army marching toward Jerusalem from the north, town by town: Aiath, Migron, Michmash, where it stores its baggage.

f.g: Baggage, supplies (not vehicles).

chapters.n: They cross the pass and camp at Geba; Ramah trembles; Gibeah, Saul’s hometown, flees.
Gallim, Laish, and poor Anathoth (Jeremiah’s hometown) cry out in alarm.
Madmenah and Gebim evacuate in panic. Each town is a few miles closer to Jerusalem.
The army halts at Nob, within sight of Jerusalem, and shakes its fist at Mount Zion.

f.g: A town just north of Jerusalem, within view of the city.

chapters.n: Then God steps in: like a forester He lops off the branches with terrifying power, felling the tall and proud. Assyria’s army was devastated before Jerusalem in 701 BC.
He cuts down the forest thickets with iron, and Lebanon’s great trees — Assyria’s might — fall before the Mighty One. Chapter 11 then shows a new shoot growing from a stump.

After Assyria’s great “forest” is cut down (chapter 20), a new shoot grows from the stump of Jesse, King David’s father. Latter-day revelation identifies the “stem of Jesse” as Christ. The angel Moroni quoted this chapter to Joseph Smith, saying it was about to be fulfilled.

f.g: A shoot or twig. D&C 113:3-4 describes it as a servant in Christ’s hands.

chapters.n: The Spirit of the Lord will rest on Him with wisdom, understanding, counsel, might, knowledge, and reverence for the Lord — the full gifts of the Spirit.

f.w: the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him

chapters.n: He delights in reverence for God, and He will not judge by appearances or hearsay, but by perfect understanding.

f.w: he shall not judge after the sight of his eyes

chapters.n: He will judge the poor fairly and defend the meek. His word — “the rod of his mouth” and “breath of his lips” — will strike the earth and destroy the wicked.

f.g: Fairness, justice.

chapters.n: Righteousness and faithfulness will be like the belt around His waist — always with Him, ready for action.

f.g: Belt or sash.
Kidneys — the inner self.

chapters.n: A vision of the Millennium: predators and prey live together in peace — wolf with lamb, leopard with goat, lion with calf — and a child leads them.

f.w: The wolf also shall dwell with the lamb

f.g: A fattened calf.

chapters.n: Cows and bears graze together, their young lie down side by side, and lions eat straw like oxen. Even nature will be transformed.

f.w: the lion shall eat straw like the ox

chapters.n: Babies will play near cobra holes, and toddlers will put their hands in a viper’s den without harm.

f.g: A venomous snake, such as a cobra.
A venomous snake or viper (KJV used a mythical creature name).

chapters.n: No one will hurt or destroy in God’s holy mountain, for the earth will be full of knowledge of the Lord, as the oceans are full of water.

f.w: the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the Lord

chapters.n: The “root of Jesse” will stand as a banner to the peoples, and the Gentiles will seek Him. Latter-day revelation describes this root as a descendant of Jesse and Joseph holding priesthood keys for the gathering.

f.g: A rallying banner.

chapters.n: The Lord will reach out “a second time” to recover His people — the first was the Exodus. He will gather the remnant from Assyria, Egypt, Ethiopia, Persia, Babylon, and distant lands. This is the latter-day gathering of Israel.

f.g: Upper (southern) Egypt.
Ethiopia/Sudan region. Elam = western Persia; Shinar = Babylonia.

chapters.n: He will raise a banner for the nations and gather Israel’s outcasts and Judah’s scattered people from the four corners of the earth.

f.w: set up an ensign for the nations

chapters.n: Ancient rivalry between Ephraim (the northern kingdom) and Judah will end. They will no longer envy or harass one another.
United, Israel will overcome old enemies — Philistines to the west, peoples of the east, Edom, Moab, and Ammon. These traditional foes symbolize all who oppose God’s people.

f.g: Neighboring nations east and south of Israel, often hostile.

chapters.n: The Lord will dry up the “tongue” (gulf) of the Egyptian sea and divide the river (the Euphrates) into seven streams so people can cross on dry ground — a new Exodus.

f.g: With dry sandals — on dry ground.

chapters.n: There will be a highway for the returning remnant, just as there was for Israel coming out of Egypt.
Isaiah 12 is a short hymn for the day of gathering. The redeemed will praise God: He was angry, but His anger has turned away and He has comforted them.

God is my salvation; I will trust and not be afraid. “The Lord JEHOVAH” is my strength and song. These words echo Moses’ song after the Red Sea. Latter-day Saints understand Jehovah to be the premortal Jesus Christ.

f.w: the Lord JEHOVAH is my strength and my song

f.g: An English form of God’s Hebrew name YHWH.

chapters.n: With joy they will draw water from the wells of salvation. Jesus later invited the thirsty to come to Him for living water.
In that day they will praise the Lord, call on His name, and tell all peoples what He has done.

f.w: declare his doings among the people

chapters.n: Sing to the Lord, for He has done marvelous things, and the whole earth knows it.
Zion’s people should shout for joy, for the Holy One of Israel dwells among them. The Millennium is pictured as God living with His people.

f.w: great is the Holy One of Israel in the midst of thee

chapters.n: Isaiah 13 is a “burden” (a weighty prophetic message of doom) against Babylon. Historically Babylon fell to the Medes and Persians in 539 BC. In scripture Babylon also symbolizes the wicked world that will fall before Christ’s coming.

f.g: Hebrew massa’ — a heavy oracle of judgment.

chapters.n: Raise a banner on a high mountain and call the armies to march through the gates of Babylon’s nobles.

f.g: Wave the hand as a signal.

chapters.n: God has commanded His consecrated warriors. The Book of Mormon reads “mine anger is not upon them that rejoice in my highness” — clarifying that God’s wrath is not against those who rejoice in Him.

f.g: Those set apart for God’s purpose — here, the armies He uses.

chapters.n: A roar of many kingdoms and nations gathering is heard in the mountains — the Lord is mustering an army for battle.

f.g: Assembles, gathers for battle.

chapters.n: They come from far away, from the ends of the heavens — the Lord and the weapons of His wrath — to destroy the land.
Wail, for the day of the Lord is near — destruction from the Almighty.

f.w: the day of the Lord is at hand

f.g: Hebrew Shaddai; a wordplay — destruction (shod) from Shaddai.

chapters.n: Every hand goes limp and every heart melts with fear.
Terror seizes them like labor pains. They stare at each other in shock, faces flushed red.
The day of the Lord comes with fierce wrath to make the land desolate and remove sinners from it.

f.w: the day of the Lord cometh

chapters.n: Stars, sun, and moon will go dark — signs Jesus also described for the last days.

f.g: Hebrew kesil — “Orion,” the hunter constellation.

chapters.n: God will punish the world’s evil and humble the arrogance of the proud and ruthless.

f.g: The pride of tyrants.

chapters.n: People will become scarcer than fine gold — rarer than the gold of Ophir.

f.g: Ophir was a distant land famed for pure gold.

chapters.n: God will shake the heavens and move the earth from its place in His fierce anger.
Like hunted gazelles or sheep without a shepherd, foreigners in Babylon will flee to their own lands.

f.g: A hunted gazelle.

chapters.n: Anyone caught will be run through; those joined to the wicked will fall by the sword. The Book of Mormon reads “every one that is proud” where the KJV has “every one that is found.”

f.g: Pierced with a spear or sword.

chapters.n: The horrors of ancient warfare are described bluntly: children killed, houses plundered, wives assaulted. Isaiah does not hide what conquest meant.

f.g: Violated, assaulted.

chapters.n: God names the attackers: the Medes, who will not be bribed with silver or gold. The Medes allied with Persia to conquer Babylon.

f.g: A people of northwestern Iran, allied with Persia under Cyrus.

chapters.n: Their archers will show no mercy, even to the young.

f.g: Children.

chapters.n: Babylon, the glory of kingdoms and pride of the Chaldeans, will be overthrown like Sodom and Gomorrah.

f.g: The Chaldeans, Babylon’s ruling people.

chapters.n: Babylon will never again be inhabited — not even nomads or shepherds will camp there. The ancient city did gradually decline into ruins.

f.g: A desert nomad.

chapters.n: Only desert creatures will live there — owls, howling animals, and “satyrs,” likely wild goats or, in folk belief, desert demons.

f.g: Howling animals, perhaps jackals.
Hebrew se‘irim — “hairy ones,” wild goats or goat-demons.

chapters.n: Jackals will howl in its palaces. Her time is near. The Book of Mormon adds a hopeful ending not in the KJV: God will destroy Babylon quickly and be merciful to His people, but the wicked will perish.

f.g: Probably jackals (Hebrew tannim).

f.w: I will be merciful unto my people
f.g: This sentence is unique to the Book of Mormon.

chapters.n: Isaiah 14 opens with mercy: the Lord will again choose Israel, settle them in their land, and foreigners will join them. Babylon’s fall makes Israel’s return possible.

f.w: the strangers shall be joined with them

chapters.n: Nations will help Israel return from the ends of the earth to their promised lands, and Israel will rule over its former oppressors. The Book of Mormon adds “from far unto the ends of the earth” and “lands of promise,” broadening the gathering.

f.w: they shall return to their lands of promise

chapters.n: The Lord will give Israel rest from sorrow, fear, and hard slavery.

f.w: the Lord shall give thee rest

chapters.n: Israel will sing a taunt-song over the king of Babylon: “How the oppressor has come to an end! The golden city is no more!”

f.g: Here a taunt-song or mocking poem.
Perhaps “the fury” or “the exactress of gold” in Hebrew.

chapters.n: The Lord has broken the staff and scepter of wicked rulers.

f.g: Rods symbolizing royal authority.

chapters.n: The tyrant who beat nations without pause and ruled in rage is now hunted himself, and no one stops it.
The whole earth is at rest and bursts into song at his fall.
Even the trees rejoice: since he fell, no woodcutter comes to chop them down. Conquerors stripped Lebanon’s forests for their building projects.

f.w: no feller is come up against us
f.g: No woodcutter comes to cut us down.

chapters.n: The underworld (Sheol) stirs to greet him. The ghosts of dead kings rise from their thrones to meet the newcomer.

f.g: Sheol — the world of the dead.

chapters.n: They mock him: “You’ve become weak like us!” Death levels the mightiest king.

f.w: Art thou also become weak as we?

chapters.n: His splendor and music are buried in the grave; maggots are his bed and worms his blanket.

“How you have fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning!” The Hebrew helel means “shining one” or “morning star.” While aimed at Babylon’s king, Latter-day Saint scripture applies it to Satan, who fell from heaven through pride.

f.w: O Lucifer, son of the morning
f.g: Latin lucifer, “light-bearer,” translates Hebrew helel ben shachar, “shining one, son of the dawn.”

chapters.n: His heart said: “I will climb to heaven, set my throne above God’s stars, and sit on the mount of assembly in the far north” — where ancient peoples imagined the gods met.

f.g: The mountain where the divine council was thought to meet.

chapters.n: “I will rise above the clouds; I will be like the Most High.” This is the essence of pride — wanting to replace God.

f.w: I will be like the Most High

chapters.n: Instead he will be brought down to Sheol, to the depths of the pit.

f.g: The farthest depths of the grave.

chapters.n: Onlookers stare and wonder: “Is this the man who shook the earth and kingdoms?”

f.g: Stare closely.

chapters.n: “Who turned the world into a wasteland, destroyed cities, and never let his prisoners go home?” Satan likewise holds his captives fast.

f.w: opened not the house of his prisoners

chapters.n: Other kings lie in honor in their own tombs.
But he is thrown out of his grave like a rejected branch, covered with the slain, a corpse trampled underfoot. Denial of burial was the ultimate disgrace.

f.g: A detested shoot or a rotten branch.

chapters.n: He will not share their honorable burial because he ruined his own land and people. The offspring of evildoers will never be famous.
His dynasty must be cut off so it cannot rise again or fill the world with its cities.

f.w: for the iniquities of their fathers

chapters.n: The Lord will rise against Babylon and wipe out its name, survivors, and descendants.

f.g: Descendant, offspring.

chapters.n: Babylon will become a swamp for wild birds, swept away by God’s broom of destruction.

f.g: A marsh bird, or possibly a hedgehog.
A broom.

chapters.n: The Lord swears that what He has planned will surely happen.

f.w: as I have purposed, so shall it stand

chapters.n: Isaiah turns back to his own day: God will crush the Assyrian on His mountains and lift Assyria’s yoke from Judah — fulfilled when Sennacherib’s army was destroyed near Jerusalem.

f.w: I will bring the Assyrian in my land

chapters.n: This is God’s plan for the whole earth; His hand is stretched out over all nations.

f.w: the hand that is stretched out upon all nations

chapters.n: When the Lord of Hosts has planned, who can cancel it? When His hand is stretched out, who can turn it back?

f.g: Cancel, make void.

chapters.n: A new oracle, dated to the year King Ahaz died (around 715 BC).
Philistia should not celebrate the death of the king who struck it. From that serpent’s root will come an even deadlier viper — a worse threat to come.

f.g: Philistia, the Philistine coastland.

chapters.n: The poorest in Israel will find food and safety, but Philistia will be destroyed by famine and the sword.

f.g: The very poorest.

chapters.n: Philistia’s gates and cities will wail as an army comes from the north like smoke, with no stragglers in its ranks.

f.g: Melts away in fear.

chapters.n: What answer will be given to messengers from other nations? That the Lord has founded Zion, and His poor and humble people will find refuge in it. Isaiah’s chapters quoted by Nephi end on this note of hope.

After the Isaiah chapters, Nephi comments. He admits Isaiah was hard for his people to understand because they didn’t know the Jewish style of prophecy — full of poetry, symbols, and references to local places.

f.w: the manner of prophesying among the Jews
f.g: Hebrew poetic style, symbolism, and historical references.

chapters.n: Nephi deliberately did not teach his people many Jewish customs, because of the wicked practices he had seen in Jerusalem.
He writes so his people, and future readers, can know that God’s judgments come upon all nations as He said.
Isaiah’s words are plain to those with the “spirit of prophecy.” But Nephi will also give his own prophecy in plain words. He loves plainness so his people can learn.
Nephi still delights in Isaiah. Having lived in Jerusalem, he knows the Jews understand their prophets best — and others can understand too if taught their context.

f.w: after the manner of the things of the Jews
f.g: With knowledge of Jewish history, geography, and culture.

chapters.n: Nephi didn’t teach his children Jewish ways, but having lived in Jerusalem he knows the region and has told his children of God’s judgments there.

f.g: The geography around Jerusalem.

chapters.n: Now Nephi gives his own plain prophecy, in which no one can be misled. When Isaiah’s prophecies are fulfilled, people will know for sure.
Isaiah’s words are valuable. Nephi wrote them for his people, who will especially understand them in the last days.
Jewish generations have suffered destruction for their wickedness, but never without warning from God’s prophets first.

f.w: save it were foretold them by the prophets

chapters.n: Right after Lehi left, destruction was foretold. They hardened their hearts, and Jerusalem was destroyed except for those taken to Babylon.
By the Spirit Nephi says they will return to Jerusalem and possess their land again.
There will be wars. Then the Only Begotten of the Father — who is also the “Father of heaven and of earth” as Creator — will come in the flesh, and they will reject Him.

f.w: the Only Begotten of the Father
the Father of heaven and of earth

chapters.n: They will crucify Him; after three days in a tomb He will rise with “healing in his wings.” All who believe will be saved. Nephi has seen His day and rejoices to prophesy of Him.

f.w: for the space of three days

chapters.n: After Christ’s resurrection and appearances, Jerusalem will be destroyed again — fulfilled by the Romans in AD 70.
The Jews will be scattered among all nations. Babylon too will be destroyed, so other nations will do the scattering.

After many generations of scattering, when they come to believe in Christ and His infinite Atonement and worship the Father in His name with pure hearts, no longer awaiting another Messiah, the time will come to gather them.
The Lord will act “a second time” to restore His people, doing a “marvelous work and a wonder.” Nephi echoes both Isaiah 11 and Isaiah 29.

f.w: a marvelous work and a wonder

chapters.n: God will bring forth His words — which will judge them at the last day — to convince them that Jesus is the true Messiah. There is only one Messiah; any other will be false.

f.w: he shall bring forth his words unto them

chapters.n: The prophets said the Messiah would come six hundred years after Lehi left Jerusalem. An angel told Nephi His name: Jesus Christ, the Son of God. “Jesus” is the Greek form of Joshua, “Jehovah saves.”

f.w: his name shall be Jesus Christ

chapters.n: Nephi swears by the God who led Israel from Egypt, healed them through the brass serpent, and gave water from the rock: there is no other name under heaven by which people can be saved but Jesus Christ.

f.w: there is none other name given under heaven
cast their eyes unto the serpent

chapters.n: God promised Nephi his writings would be preserved and passed down, so the promise to Joseph — that his seed would never perish — could be fulfilled.

f.w: the promise may be fulfilled unto Joseph

chapters.n: These records will last as long as the earth, and nations that receive them will be judged by them.

A famous verse: Nephi writes to persuade people to believe in Christ and be reconciled to God, knowing “it is by grace that we are saved, after all we can do.” Grace is not a reward for effort; our faithful effort is how we receive the gift Christ freely offers.

f.w: it is by grace that we are saved

f.g: Often understood as “in addition to” or “even after” all we can do — grace is always essential.

chapters.n: Though they believe in Christ, the Nephites keep the law of Moses, looking steadily forward to Christ until the law is fulfilled.

f.w: we keep the law of Moses

chapters.n: The law was given to point to Christ. It is “dead” to them as a means of salvation; they are made alive in Christ through faith. They keep it because God commanded it.

f.w: the law hath become dead unto us

chapters.n: One of the most beloved verses in the Book of Mormon: “we talk of Christ, we rejoice in Christ, we preach of Christ, we prophesy of Christ,” so their children will know where to turn for forgiveness of sins.

f.g: Forgiveness; release from sin’s penalty.

chapters.n: They teach about the law so their children will see its limits and look to the life found in Christ — and not harden their hearts when the law is fulfilled and ends.

f.w: after the law is fulfilled in Christ

chapters.n: Because the Nephites are stubborn, Nephi has spoken plainly so they can’t misunderstand. The right way is to believe in Christ and not deny Him; to deny Him is to deny the prophets and the law.

f.g: Stubborn, unwilling to bend.

f.w: the right way is to believe in Christ

chapters.n: Christ is the Holy One of Israel. Worship Him with all your might, mind, strength, and soul, and you will never be cast out.

f.w: Christ is the Holy One of Israel
with all your might, mind, and strength

chapters.n: Until the law of Moses is fulfilled, they must keep its rites and ordinances.

f.g: The sacrifices and rituals of the law of Moses.

chapters.n: Nephi prophesies that after His resurrection Christ will show Himself to Nephi’s descendants, and His words will become their law — fulfilled in 3 Nephi.

f.w: he shall show himself unto you
shall be the law which ye shall do

chapters.n: Nephi has seen that many generations will pass with great wars among his people.
There will be signs of Christ’s birth, death, and resurrection. The wicked who kill prophets and saints will perish, for the blood of the innocent cries to God from the ground, as Abel’s did.

f.w: signs given unto my people of his birth
the cry of the blood of the saints

chapters.n: The proud and wicked will burn like stubble on that day — words also found in Malachi.
Those who kill prophets and saints will be swallowed by the earth, buried by mountains, swept away by whirlwinds, and crushed by falling buildings — a preview of the destruction in 3 Nephi 8–9.

f.w: the depths of the earth shall swallow them up

chapters.n: Thunder, lightning, earthquakes, and destruction will come; the Lord’s fiery anger will consume them like stubble.
Nephi feels deep anguish over the slain among his people — it nearly overwhelms him — yet he affirms: “Thy ways are just.”
Those who heed the prophets, don’t persecute them, and look steadfastly to Christ despite persecution will not perish.

f.w: look forward unto Christ with steadfastness

chapters.n: The “Son of Righteousness” will heal them, and they will have peace for three generations and much of the fourth — the golden age described in 4 Nephi.
Afterward swift destruction will come. Nephi has seen it with pain. His people will “sell themselves for naught,” choosing pride and darkness over light.
The Spirit will not strive with people forever. When it withdraws, destruction quickly follows. This grieves Nephi.

f.w: the Spirit of the Lord will not always strive with man

chapters.n: Just as the Jews must be convinced that Jesus is the Christ, the Gentiles must be too — that He is the Eternal God.

f.w: Jesus is the Christ, the Eternal God
f.g: Echoed on the Book of Mormon title page.

chapters.n: Christ reveals Himself by the Holy Ghost to all believers in every nation, working miracles according to their faith.
Nephi now prophesies about the last days, when God will bring these records forth.

After Lehi’s descendants dwindle in unbelief and are struck down by the Gentiles — besieged and brought low — the words of the righteous will still be written, the prayers of the faithful heard, and the fallen not forgotten.

f.w: laid siege against them with a mount
the prayers of the faithful shall be heard

chapters.n: The destroyed will speak from the ground, their voices whispering out of the dust — a description of a buried record coming forth. Nephi adapts Isaiah 29:4.

f.w: their speech shall whisper out of the dust

f.g: Here, a voice that seems to come from the past.

chapters.n: They will write what happens among them, and it will be sealed in a book. Those who dwindle in unbelief will not have it, because they would destroy it.
The destruction will be sudden; the terrible ones will blow away like chaff in an instant.
Those who dwindle in unbelief will be struck by the Gentiles.

f.w: smitten by the hand of the Gentiles

chapters.n: The Gentiles, proud in their own eyes, will stumble over a great obstacle: they build many churches but deny God’s power and miracles, preaching their own learning for profit and oppressing the poor.

f.w: put down the power and miracles of God

chapters.n: Many churches will stir envy, conflict, and malice — division rather than unity.

Secret combinations will exist, as in ancient times, founded by the devil. He leads people gently by the neck with a thin flaxen cord, then binds them forever with strong cords. Sin begins small and becomes slavery.

f.g: A thin linen thread — easily broken at first.

chapters.n: In contrast to the devil’s secret works, the Lord God does not work in darkness.

f.w: the Lord God worketh not in darkness

chapters.n: Everything God does benefits the world. He loves the world so much that He gave His life to draw all people to Him. He forbids no one His salvation.

f.w: that he may draw all men unto him

chapters.n: Does He tell anyone to go away? No — He invites all the ends of the earth to come and receive His blessings freely, without money or price.
Has He ever commanded anyone to leave places of worship? No — He welcomes all.

f.g: Jewish places of assembly and worship.

chapters.n: Has He forbidden anyone His salvation? No. It is free for all, and He commands His people to invite all to repent.

f.w: he hath given it free for all men

chapters.n: Has He kept anyone from His goodness? No. All have equal privilege; none are forbidden.

f.w: all men are privileged the one like unto the other

chapters.n: He forbids priestcraft — preaching to make oneself a light to the world for money and praise, without seeking Zion’s welfare.

f.g: Using religion for personal profit or popularity.

chapters.n: Instead He commands charity — love. Without charity people are nothing. With it, they would never let a worker in Zion go without.
Those who labor in Zion must work for Zion, not for money; working for money alone leads to ruin.

f.w: if they labor for money they shall perish

chapters.n: God commands people not to murder, lie, steal, take His name in vain, envy, hold malice, quarrel, or commit sexual sin. Those who do will perish.

f.w: that they should not contend one with another
take the name of the Lord their God in vain

chapters.n: None of these sins come from the Lord. He does only good, makes everything plain, invites everyone, and denies none who come — “black and white, bond and free, male and female… all are alike unto God.” This verse is a cornerstone of the Church’s teaching on the equal worth of every person.

f.g: Those who do not know God’s law; He remembers them too.

chapters.n: Nephi now applies Isaiah 29 to the last days. He widens the prophecy beyond Jerusalem: Gentiles and Jews everywhere, including those in the Americas, will be “drunken” with wickedness before the Lord sets things right.

f.g: A metaphor: sin that dulls judgment the way alcohol does.

chapters.n: Judgments of nature—thunder, earthquake, storm, fire—will visit the wicked. Isaiah’s original words described Jerusalem’s siege; Nephi sees a larger fulfillment at the end of the world.

f.g: “Lord of armies”—God as commander of heaven’s forces.

chapters.n: Nations that attack Zion will be like a hungry man who dreams of a feast and wakes up still starving. Their schemes to destroy God’s people will come to nothing.

f.g: The holy mount of Jerusalem; in latter-day usage also the gathered, covenant people of God.

chapters.n: The wicked will be stunned and stagger as if drunk—not from wine, but from spiritual confusion they brought on themselves.

f.g: Stop short and be astonished.

chapters.n: Because people closed their eyes and rejected the prophets, God let a “deep sleep” settle over them, and their seers were taken away. Spiritual blindness follows refusing light.

f.g: Prophets who see spiritual realities, past or future; compare Mosiah 8:15-17.

chapters.n: Into that sleepy world God will bring “the words of a book” written by people now dead. Latter-day Saints understand this as the Book of Mormon, written by ancient prophets.

f.g: Those who have died—here the Nephite prophets whose record speaks from the dust.

chapters.n: Part of the book will be sealed, containing a revelation of the whole history of the world from beginning to end.

f.w: from the beginning of the world to the ending thereof

chapters.n: The sealed portion will be withheld while the world is wicked. God reveals greater truths only when people are ready to receive them.

f.w: the book shall be kept from them

chapters.n: The book will be given to one man, who will pass some of its words to another. This matches Joseph Smith giving a copy of characters to Martin Harris.

f.w: he shall deliver these words unto another

chapters.n: The man will not hand over the book or its sealed portion. It stays sealed by God’s power until the Lord’s own timing.

f.w: own due time of the Lord
f.g: The time God himself chooses.

chapters.n: A day will come when the sealed words are read openly, “upon the house tops,” and everything that has ever happened among humanity will be made known.

The book will be hidden from the public, but three witnesses besides the translator will see it by God’s power and testify of it. This was fulfilled in Oliver Cowdery, David Whitmer, and Martin Harris.
A few others will also see it as God allows, to add their testimony. The Eight Witnesses handled the plates and wrote their own statement.

f.g: Fulfilled in part by the Eight Witnesses, whose testimony appears in the front of the Book of Mormon.

f.w: as if it were from the dead

chapters.n: God establishes truth through multiple witnesses, and warns those who reject his word. The principle of witnesses runs throughout scripture.

f.w: in the mouth of as many witnesses

chapters.n: The unsealed words will be shown to a learned man who asks for the book itself. Latter-day Saints connect this with Martin Harris showing the characters to scholar Charles Anthon in 1828.
Nephi exposes the learned man’s motive: worldly reputation and profit, not God’s glory.

f.g: To make money or advantage for oneself.

chapters.n: The man explains that the book cannot be brought because it is sealed.
The learned man answers, “I cannot read it”—Anthon’s reported reply to Martin Harris was nearly the same.
So God gives the book to a man who is not learned—Joseph Smith, a young farmer with little schooling—who humbly admits his lack of learning.
God reassures him: the scholars have rejected the work, but God can do it himself. The unlearned man will read words God gives him—translation by divine gift, not scholarship.

f.w: I am able to do mine own work

chapters.n: The translator must leave the sealed portion alone. God will bring it out when he chooses, proving he can do his own work.

f.w: Touch not the things which are sealed

chapters.n: After translating and showing the plates to the witnesses, the man must return the book into God’s keeping. Joseph Smith gave the plates back to the angel Moroni.
God declares he is a God of miracles, unchanging across time, and that he works among people according to their faith.

f.w: the same yesterday, today, and forever

chapters.n: Nephi introduces another message the Lord will give to the man who reads the book.
People honor God with their words but their hearts are far away, and their reverence comes from human traditions. Jesus quoted this verse, and the Lord echoed it to Joseph Smith in the First Vision.

f.w: draw near unto me with their mouth

chapters.n: Because of this, God will do “a marvelous work and a wonder”—the restoration of the gospel—that will outshine the wisdom of the worldly wise.
Those who plot in secret think no one sees them. God compares them to clay telling the potter he doesn’t exist. The creation cannot outsmart its Creator.

f.g: Twisting matters, perverting what is right.

chapters.n: Soon the land itself will be transformed: Lebanon’s forest becomes a fruitful field. Many read this as a picture of the gathering and renewal of Israel in the last days.

f.w: Lebanon shall be turned into a fruitful field

chapters.n: Those who were spiritually deaf and blind will hear and see through the book. The Book of Mormon brings light out of obscurity.

f.w: out of obscurity and out of darkness

chapters.n: The humble and the poor will find joy in the Lord. The gospel is good news especially for the meek.

f.g: A favorite title of Isaiah for God; Nephites understood it as Christ (2 Nephi 25:29).

chapters.n: The tyrant and the mocker will be brought down, and those who look for chances to do evil will be removed.

f.g: The ruthless oppressor.
One who mocks sacred things.

chapters.n: Also judged: those who trap people over a single word, ensnare the one who rebukes evil at the city gate, and deny justice to the righteous over trivial excuses.

f.g: The city gate was where court was held; this is the honest judge or witness.
For nothing; on a flimsy pretext.

chapters.n: The Lord who redeemed Abraham promises that Jacob—Israel personified—will no longer be ashamed or pale with fear.

f.g: Turn pale, as from shame or fear.

chapters.n: When Israel sees its descendants gathered and faithful, they will honor God’s holy name together.
Those who were confused will understand, and complainers will learn true doctrine—a hopeful ending showing what the book will accomplish.
Nephi says he has spoken as the Spirit pressed him to, so he is certain these prophecies will be fulfilled.

f.g: Urged or compelled from within.

chapters.n: The book that comes forth will be priceless to everyone, but especially to Lehi’s descendants, a remnant of Israel who will learn of their heritage through it.

f.w: remnant of the house of Israel

chapters.n: In the last days many churches will be founded by people, not by the Lord, each claiming, “I am the Lord’s!” The repeated “I, I” captures the rivalry.

f.w: built up, and not unto the Lord

chapters.n: These churches will argue with each other. Their ministers will rely on their own learning and deny the Holy Ghost, who is the true source of inspired speech.

f.g: Gives inspired words to speak.

chapters.n: They deny God’s power, teaching that God has finished his work and handed his authority over to humans, so he no longer acts today.
A key false teaching: miracles have ceased. Moroni later answers this directly—if miracles stop, it is because faith has stopped.

f.w: he is not a God of miracles

chapters.n: Some will preach pure pleasure-seeking: live it up, for death ends everything. This echoes an attitude Isaiah and Paul both condemned.
Others will teach that small sins don’t matter—a little lying or cheating—because God will give a light punishment and save everyone anyway. Nephi calls this a dangerous lie.

f.w: dig a pit for thy neighbor
f.g: Set a trap for someone; scheme to harm them.

f.w: beat us with a few stripes
f.g: Punish lightly, like a few lashes.

chapters.n: Many teachers will spread such foolish doctrines, swelled with pride, and try to hide their plans from God.

f.g: Swollen with pride.

f.w: hide their counsels from the Lord

chapters.n: The blood of faithful martyrs cries out against these false teachers, like Abel’s blood crying from the ground.
A short lament: all have wandered off the path and become corrupt.
Nephi names the causes: pride, false teachers, and false doctrine. Proud churches become corrupt.

f.g: Exalted in pride.

chapters.n: Churches spend on luxurious buildings and fine clothes while neglecting the poor, and they look down on the humble. Mormon saw the same in our day.
Most have gone astray, except a few humble followers of Christ—and even they sometimes err because they’ve been taught human ideas instead of revealed truth.

f.g: Stubbornness, like an ox that won’t bend to the yoke.

chapters.n: A triple “wo” on the proud wise, learned, and rich, on false preachers, and on the immoral—those who twist the Lord’s straight path.

f.g: A threefold lament—the strongest warning of coming sorrow.

chapters.n: Woe to those who deny justice and mock what is good. When the wicked are fully ripe in sin, God’s judgment will come quickly.

f.w: turn aside the just for a thing of naught

chapters.n: But repentance changes everything: if people turn from wickedness, they will not be destroyed. God’s warnings are invitations.

f.w: if the inhabitants of the earth shall repent

chapters.n: The “great and abominable church”—everything that fights against God—must fall with a great crash.

f.w: great must be the fall thereof

chapters.n: The devil’s kingdom will be shaken. Its members will either be stirred to repent or stirred to anger and be bound in the devil’s chains.
Satan’s first tactic: stir people up with rage against everything good.
His second tactic is gentler: lull people into feeling spiritually safe—“All is well in Zion”—and lead them “carefully” to hell, one comfortable step at a time.

f.g: False safety based on worldly comfort and prosperity.

chapters.n: His third tactic is flattery: telling people there is no hell and no devil. Disbelief in him makes his work easier.
Death, hell, and the devil will all stand before God’s judgment. Those who chose evil receive the “lake of fire and brimstone,” a vivid image of the anguish of soul in being cut off from God.
A sharp warning against complacency among God’s own people.
Woe to anyone who shouts “All is well!” when it isn’t—echoing verse 21.
Woe to those who follow human philosophies and deny God’s power and the gift of the Holy Ghost.
Woe to those who say they have all the revelation they need. Closing the canon closes the heart.
Those angry at truth will tremble. Someone built on the rock welcomes new truth gladly; someone on sand fears it will topple him.
Nephi repeats the warning against claiming we already have enough of God’s word. This prophetically addresses the objection “A Bible! We have got a Bible.”
God teaches step by step—line upon line. Those who receive light gain more; those who refuse lose even what they had. Revelation is ongoing and grows with obedience.

f.w: line upon line, precept upon precept
unto him that receiveth I will give more

chapters.n: Trusting in human strength or wisdom alone is a curse, unless that counsel comes by the Holy Ghost.

f.g: Relies on human power instead of God.

chapters.n: The Gentiles will often reject God, yet he keeps reaching out his arm “all the day long.” If they repent, he will be merciful—a closing note of patient love.
Nephi quotes the Lord: in the day of his “marvelous work,” God will reach out “the second time” to recover scattered Israel. The sentence continues into the following verses.
God remembers his promises to Lehi and Nephi that their descendants’ words would reach their own posterity and spread worldwide as a rallying flag for Israel.

f.g: Whistle or call out; an image of a shepherd whistling to gather a flock.
A banner or flag that people rally around.

chapters.n: Many Gentiles will object, “A Bible! A Bible! We have got a Bible, and there cannot be any more Bible.” This was a common reaction when the Book of Mormon appeared in 1830.
The Lord answers sharply. The Bible came from the Jews, yet how have Gentiles thanked them for their sacrifices in preserving it?

f.g: Painful, exhausting labor.

chapters.n: Instead of gratitude, many Gentiles have cursed and hated the Jews. God says he has not forgotten his people and will hold persecutors accountable—a strong rebuke of antisemitism.

f.w: I the Lord have not forgotten my people

chapters.n: The Lord calls anyone a fool who claims the Bible is all there is—especially since they only have it thanks to the Jews.
God created all people everywhere, including those on distant “isles of the sea,” and he speaks to every nation. It makes sense he would have other records.

Two nations’ testimonies—the Bible from the Jews and the Book of Mormon from the Nephites—together witness that God is real and treats all nations alike. When they “run together,” they strengthen each other.

f.g: Join and agree, like streams merging.

chapters.n: God is unchanging, and he speaks when he chooses. Saying one word doesn’t stop him from saying another; his work goes on forever.

f.w: the same yesterday, today, and forever
my work is not yet finished

chapters.n: Having the Bible doesn’t mean it holds all of God’s words; he has caused more to be written.
God commands people everywhere to write what he reveals, and the world will be judged out of these books.

f.w: out of the books which shall be written I will judge the world

chapters.n: The Jews, the Nephites, the scattered tribes of Israel, and all nations will each record God’s words to them.

f.w: other tribes of the house of Israel

chapters.n: Eventually these records will be shared among all these peoples, each gaining the others’ scripture.

f.g: The northern tribes taken captive by Assyria around 722 BC, whose later history is unknown.

chapters.n: Israel will be gathered home and God’s word gathered “in one.” This fulfills God’s covenant to remember Abraham’s descendants forever.

f.w: my word also shall be gathered in one

chapters.n: Nephi warns his own people not to feel superior to the Gentiles. Being of Israel’s lineage saves no one; only keeping the commandments does.
Any Gentile who repents becomes part of God’s covenant people, while unrepentant Israelites are cut off. Covenant belonging depends on faith in Christ, not ancestry.

f.g: Here explicitly identified with God’s Son, Jesus Christ.

chapters.n: After the book comes forth and is sealed up again, many Gentiles will believe it and take it to Lehi’s descendants.

f.w: carry them forth unto the remnant of our seed

chapters.n: Through it, Lehi’s descendants will learn their origin: that their ancestors left Jerusalem and that they are of Israelite descent.

f.g: Here meaning people from the kingdom of Judah; Lehi was of Joseph’s tribe through Manasseh (Alma 10:3).

chapters.n: They will be taught the gospel of Jesus Christ and regain the knowledge of Christ their forefathers once had.
They will rejoice to see this as God’s blessing. Spiritual “scales of darkness” will fall from their eyes, and they will become a pure and delightsome people.

f.g: Delightful, pleasing—here to God, in faithfulness.

chapters.n: Scattered Jews will also begin to believe in Christ and gather, and believers will likewise become delightsome to God.

f.w: gather in upon the face of the land

chapters.n: God will begin a worldwide work among every nation, people, and language to restore his people.
Nephi now quotes Isaiah 11: the Lord will judge the poor fairly and defend the meek. His word alone—“the rod of his mouth”—will defeat the wicked.

f.g: Fairness, justice.

chapters.n: Nephi inserts his own explanation into Isaiah’s words: a great division is coming. The Lord will spare the righteous even if the wicked must be destroyed by fire.
Righteousness and faithfulness will be like a belt the Messiah wears—his defining qualities, always with him.

f.g: Reins = kidneys or inner self; the girdle is a belt. Faithfulness binds him through and through.

chapters.n: Predators and prey will live together in peace, led by a little child—a picture of the peaceful Millennium.

f.w: the wolf dwell with the lamb

f.g: A young animal fattened for food.

chapters.n: Even the cow and bear will graze together, and the lion will eat straw—violence removed from creation itself.

f.w: the lion shall eat straw like the ox

chapters.n: An infant could play by a snake’s hole without harm. Enmity between humans and serpents, begun in Eden, will end.

f.g: A venomous snake.
A legendary deadly serpent; here a poisonous viper.

chapters.n: Nothing will hurt or destroy, because the earth will be as full of the knowledge of God as the ocean is full of water.

f.w: as the waters cover the sea

f.g: God’s temple-mount and, by extension, his kingdom.

chapters.n: Leaving Isaiah, Nephi adds that in that day the history and secrets of all nations will be made known.

f.w: all things shall be made known

chapters.n: Every secret will come to light and every sealed thing will be opened, including the sealed portion of the book.
Everything God has revealed will be revealed again, and Satan will lose his power over hearts for a long time—the thousand years of peace. Nephi ends this sermon.

f.w: Satan shall have power over the hearts of the children of men no more

chapters.n: Nephi, now old, finishes his prophesying. He can record only a little of what he knows and only a few of his brother Jacob’s words.
He has one last thing to teach: “the doctrine of Christ.” He promises to speak plainly.
Nephi loves plain teaching because that is how God works—speaking to people in their own language so they can understand.

f.w: according to their language, unto their understanding

chapters.n: He reminds readers of his earlier vision of John the Baptist, who would baptize Jesus, “the Lamb of God.”
If sinless Jesus needed baptism “to fulfil all righteousness,” how much more do we, who are not holy, need it.
Nephi asks a teaching question: in what way did Jesus fulfill all righteousness through baptism?
Though holy, Jesus humbled himself before the Father and showed his commitment to obey. His baptism was an act of humility and covenant, setting the pattern for us.
After his baptism, the Holy Ghost came upon him in the form of a dove—showing that baptism by water is followed by the Spirit.

f.w: in the form of a dove

chapters.n: His example shows how narrow the path and gate are—the specific, exact way into God’s kingdom.

f.g: Strait = narrow, tight (not “straight”).

chapters.n: Jesus invites, “Follow thou me.” Following him means being willing to keep the Father’s commandments.
Nephi heard the Father’s own voice commanding repentance and baptism in the name of his Son.
The Son also spoke to Nephi: those baptized in his name will receive the Holy Ghost just as he did. Nephi heard both Father and Son—they are distinct voices united in one message.

f.w: do the things which ye have seen me do

chapters.n: Sincere followers who repent and take Christ’s name through baptism receive the “baptism of fire and of the Holy Ghost,” which purifies them and lets them speak with heavenly power.
The Son warns: if, after all this light and these covenants, someone denies him, it would have been better never to have known him. Greater light brings greater accountability.

f.w: better for you that ye had not known me

chapters.n: The Father confirms the Son’s words are true and adds the key requirement: endure to the end.

f.w: He that endureth to the end

chapters.n: Nephi concludes that salvation requires lifelong following of Christ, not just a good start.
Nephi summarizes: the gate is repentance and baptism by water, followed by a remission of sins through the Holy Ghost’s purifying fire.

f.w: the gate by which ye should enter

f.g: Forgiveness; release from the debt of sin.

chapters.n: Entering the gate puts you on the strait and narrow path to eternal life, and the Holy Ghost testifies of the Father and Son as promised.
Is getting on the path enough? No. We got there only through Christ’s word, unwavering faith, and complete reliance on his merits—not our own.
So keep pressing forward, steady in Christ, full of hope and love, feasting on his word, and enduring to the end. The Father promises eternal life.

f.w: feasting upon the word of Christ

chapters.n: This is the only way and Christ’s is the only saving name. Nephi calls it the true doctrine of the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost—three persons united as one God in purpose.
Nephi senses his readers wondering what to do next after entering the gate. He gently asks why they are puzzled—he has already given the answer.
He reminds them: after receiving the Holy Ghost they can speak with the “tongue of angels”—which is only possible through the Holy Ghost.
Angels speak Christ’s words by the Holy Ghost. So feast on Christ’s words—through scripture and the Spirit—and they will tell you everything you need to do.

f.w: feast upon the words of Christ
tell you all things what ye should do

chapters.n: If anyone still doesn’t understand, it’s because they haven’t asked or knocked. Light is available but must be sought.

f.w: ask not, neither do ye knock

chapters.n: Nephi repeats: enter by the gate, receive the Holy Ghost, and it will show you all things you should do.

f.w: it will show unto you all things

chapters.n: This is the doctrine of Christ; no more will be given until Christ appears in the flesh among them—which happened in 3 Nephi—and then they must obey what he says.

f.w: manifest himself unto you in the flesh

chapters.n: The Spirit stops Nephi from saying more. He mourns that people will not seek or accept knowledge even when it is taught as plainly as possible.

f.g: Stubborn refusal to bend or be taught.

chapters.n: Nephi grieves that some still hesitate. The Spirit teaches us to pray; the evil spirit teaches us not to. That alone shows which influence to follow.

f.w: the evil spirit teacheth not a man to pray

chapters.n: Pray always and don’t give up. Before doing anything for the Lord, pray that the Father will consecrate it—make it holy and beneficial for your soul.

f.g: Dedicate and make sacred.

chapters.n: Nephi admits he can’t write everything, and that writing is weaker than spoken words, which the Holy Ghost carries into listeners’ hearts.

f.w: neither am I mighty in writing

chapters.n: Many harden themselves against the Spirit and so dismiss written scripture as worthless.

f.g: Worthless things, nothing.

chapters.n: Yet Nephi treasures what he wrote. He prays for his people by day and weeps for them at night, confident God hears him.
God will consecrate his prayers, and his weak words will be made strong. His record persuades people to do good, tells of their ancestors, and testifies of Jesus.

f.w: written in weakness will be made strong

chapters.n: His words speak bluntly against sin. Only someone influenced by the devil will be angry at plain truth.
A beloved line: Nephi rejoices in plainness, in truth, and in “my Jesus,” who rescued his soul. His whole record points here.

f.g: Rejoice, take pride in.

chapters.n: Nephi loves his people and trusts in Christ that many will stand clean before him at judgment.
He loves the Jews too, as the people he came from.

f.g: Lehi’s family came from Jerusalem in the kingdom of Judah.

chapters.n: He also loves the Gentiles. But for all groups, hope lies only in being reconciled to Christ and staying on the narrow path until life’s probation ends.

f.g: Mortal life as a time of testing and preparation.

chapters.n: Nephi appeals to everyone: believe in Christ. If you truly believe in Christ, you will believe these words, because they are his.
If anyone doubts, judgment day will settle it: Christ himself will confirm these are his words, and Nephi and his reader will stand face to face before him.

f.w: face to face before his bar

f.g: The judge’s bench; a place of judgment.

chapters.n: Nephi prays that many, if not all, will be saved in God’s kingdom.
He bids farewell to Israel and the whole world as “one crying from the dust”—a voice from the grave through the book—until the great judgment day.
To those who reject God’s goodness and the words of the Jews, of Nephi, and of Christ, he says an everlasting farewell: these words will stand as witness against them.
What Nephi seals on earth will be used at the judgment bar. He obeys God’s command and closes with “Amen.” Nephi’s writings end here; Jacob’s begin next.
